lead: Both readings today are full of chains. Hebrews finishes its roll of the faithful with people in prison, under the sword and in hiding, whom no chain could part from God. Mark shows a man whom no chain could hold, living among the tombs, until Jesus steps out of a boat and the man is sitting there clothed and in his right mind. The key words are faith, witness and mercy. The response to Psalm 31 sums up the day: “Be strong, and let your heart take courage, all you who wait for the Lord.”

r.h: Of whom the world was not worthy
set: Hebrews 11 is the great roll of faith, from Abel onward. In these last verses the author says that time would fail him, and he stops telling stories one by one. He only hints at them, and his first readers would have known them from the Scriptures: Gideon, Barak, Samson and Jephthah from the Book of Judges, David and Samuel, Daniel among the lions, and the mothers who received their children back through Elijah and Elisha (1 Kings 17:17–24; 2 Kings 4:18–37).
str: v. 32: names, and the author's confession that there is no time for them all.
vv. 33–35a: faith that won: kingdoms, lions, fire, the dead restored.
vv. 35b–38: faith that seemed to lose: torture, prison, stones, the saw, life in caves.
vv. 39–40: none of them received the promise yet, because God had us in view as well.
kw: The verb comes from tympanon, a drum, and seems to mean beating a victim stretched out on a frame. The same noun appears in the account of old Eleazar (2 Maccabees 6:19, 28), and the “better resurrection” recalls the seven brothers and their mother (2 Maccabees 7).
Literally “having been witnessed to”. God and the Scriptures bear witness to these people. The next verses call them a “cloud of witnesses” (12:1), using the noun from which our word “martyr” comes.
A favourite word of Hebrews, which keeps speaking of a better hope, a better covenant and a better sacrifice. The “better” here is what Christ has brought.
vv: Women received their dead by resurrection. Others were tortured, refusing to accept release, in order to obtain a better resurrection.
The two sentences stand side by side on purpose. Some were given their dead back for a time. Others could have bought their lives and refused. Faith does not always look like a rescue.
They were stoned to death, they were sawn in two, they were killed by the sword;

The Old Testament tells of the stoning of Zechariah (2 Chronicles 24:20–21). The Scriptures do not tell of anyone being sawn in two; a later Jewish tradition says that this was the death of the prophet Isaiah under King Manasseh.
of whom the world was not worthy.
The usual way of judging is turned upside down. The world thought these people unfit to live among them. Scripture says that the world was not fit to have them.
since God had provided something better so that they would not, apart from us, be made perfect.
A remarkable ending. The heroes of Israel wait for us, and we need them. God's people are one family, and all reach the goal together in Christ.
ch: The Catechism turns to this “cloud of witnesses” when it says that the believer never walks alone in faith (CCC 165), and it calls martyrdom the supreme witness to the truth of the faith (CCC 2473). The Second Vatican Council recalls the ancient saying that the universal Church will gather all the just “from Abel, the just one, to the last of the elect” (Lumen Gentium 2). Verse 40 says the same in its own way.

r.h: Clothed and in his right mind
set: Saturday's Gospel ended with the calming of the storm on the way across the lake (4:35–41). Now the boat lands on the eastern side, in the region of the Decapolis, a league of Greek-speaking cities. The people here are largely Gentile, which is why there can be a herd of swine (compare Leviticus 11:7). The manuscripts differ over the place name: “Gerasenes” in Mark, “Gadarenes” in Matthew 8:28, and “Gergesenes” in some copies. Gerasa itself lay well inland, so the exact site cannot be fixed. Mark's interest lies elsewhere.
str: vv. 1–5: the man among the tombs.
vv. 6–13: the meeting, the name, and the swine.
vv. 14–17: the people come, see him healed, and ask Jesus to leave.
vv. 18–20: the man wants to follow, and is sent home to tell.
kw: A Latin word carried into Greek: the Roman army's largest unit, several thousand men. The name says how many powers hold him. Some scholars also hear in it an allusion to the Roman occupation; Mark does not develop this.
Sound-minded, self-possessed. The man who was howling on the mountains is now sitting quietly, the posture of a disciple.
The same root as eleison in “Kyrie eleison”. Jesus names what has happened to the man in one word: mercy.
vv: Night and day among the tombs and on the mountains he was always howling and bruising himself with stones.
Mark piles up the details of a life destroyed: cut off from people, living with the dead, and hurting himself. Evil is pictured here as what it does: it isolates and it wounds.
Then Jesus asked him, “What is your name?” He replied, “My name is Legion; for we are many.”
The man has lost even his name. When asked who he is, he can only say what possesses him.
“Go home to your friends, and tell them how much the Lord has done for you, and what mercy he has shown you.”
Elsewhere Mark's Jesus often asks for silence (1:44; 5:43). Here, in Gentile country, he sends the man out to speak.
And he went away and began to proclaim in the Decapolis how much Jesus had done for him;
Notice the shift: Jesus said “the Lord”, and the man says “Jesus”. He has understood. The first preacher to the cities of the Decapolis is a man who was not allowed to get into the boat.
ch: The Catechism says that Jesus' exorcisms release people from the domination of demons and anticipate his great victory over “the ruler of this world” (CCC 550). The Church has received from him the power and office of exorcizing, and a simple form of exorcism is part of every Baptism. She also teaches that illness, especially psychological illness, is a very different matter, and that treating it is the concern of medical science (CCC 1673).

qa: Was it fair that the herd of swine was destroyed?

Mark does not explain this. It is usual to note two things. The destruction shows what the unclean spirits wanted to do to the man, and what they do to anything they enter. And the story measures one man against two thousand animals and finds him worth more. The sad part comes after: the people see the man healed and ask Jesus to go.
study: The man wanted to get into the boat, and Jesus sent him home. Where is Jesus sending me, when I would rather be somewhere else?
“Of whom the world was not worthy.” Which Christians suffering for their faith in many lands can I remember in prayer today, along with those who wrong them?

lead: Forty days after Christmas the Church goes to the Temple with Mary and Joseph, with candles in her hands. Malachi promised that the Lord would suddenly come to his temple, and Psalm 24 tells the ancient gates to lift up their heads for the King of glory. When the King does come, nobody opens any gates. A poor couple carries him in, with two birds for the offering, and only two old people recognize him. Hebrews, the alternative first reading, explains why he comes this way: he shared our flesh and blood, in order to set us at liberty from the fear of death. And an old man with the child in his arms says that he is now ready to die in peace. The key words are coming, offering and light.

r.h: Malachi: the Lord whom you seek
set: Malachi speaks after the exile, probably in the fifth century BC. The Temple has been rebuilt, but the priests offer blemished animals (1:8) and the people are weary of waiting. They ask, “Where is the God of justice?” (2:17). Chapter 3 answers: he is coming, and he is coming to the very place where worship has gone wrong.
The Lectionary offers two choices for the first reading today, and when the feast falls on a Sunday both are read. Both are treated here.
str: v. 1: the messenger who prepares the way, and then the Lord himself.
v. 2: the question: who can endure it? The images of fire and soap.
v. 3: he will purify the descendants of Levi.
v. 4: the result: offerings pleasing to the Lord.
kw: Almost always used in the Old Testament of something unexpected, often an unexpected disaster. God's visit cannot be scheduled. On this feast the surprise is of another kind: no one expected a baby.
Israel's sanctuary, the same word used of a king's palace. The Lord comes to it as a king to his own house. “His temple” is the point of the phrase.
Found only here. Christians hear in the “messenger” who prepares the way John the Baptist (Mark 1:2; Matthew 11:10), and in “the Lord” who follows him Jesus himself.
vv: See, I am sending my messenger to prepare the way before me, and the Lord whom you seek will suddenly come to his temple.
“Whom you seek” has an edge to it. The people have been complaining that God is absent. They may not be ready for what they ask for.
But who can endure the day of his coming, and who can stand when he appears? For he is like a refiner’s fire and like fullers’ soap;
The refiner melts silver to take the waste from it, and the fuller uses a strong soap to clean new cloth. Both are hard on the material, and both are done because it is valuable.
he will sit as a refiner and purifier of silver, and he will purify the descendants of Levi
The refiner sits, because the work takes patience and attention. The cleansing begins with the priests, in the house of God itself. Then the offerings will again be right (3:4).
ch: The Gospels apply Malachi 3:1 to John the Baptist, so the Church reads it as a promise of Christ. Today it is read beside Luke 2, where the Lord enters his temple for the first time. The Catechism says that Jesus showed the deepest respect for the Temple, where Joseph and Mary presented him forty days after his birth (CCC 583). The refining fire is not forgotten. Simeon's words about the falling and rising of many (Luke 2:34) carry the same note.

r.h: Hebrews: he had to become like us
set: Hebrews opens by showing that the Son is far above the angels (chapter 1). Chapter 2 then says something surprising: for a little while he was made lower than they, in order to suffer and to bring many children to glory (2:9–10). These verses give the reason. They also use the title “high priest” for Jesus for the first time in the letter, and it will be its great theme.
str: vv. 14–15: he shared flesh and blood to destroy death's power and release those enslaved by fear.
v. 16: he came to help the descendants of Abraham, not angels.
v. 17: so he had to be like us: a merciful and faithful high priest.
v. 18: because he was tested, he can help those who are tested.
kw: The Greek has “blood and flesh”, a biblical way of speaking of human life in its weakness. The Son did not merely appear to be human. The Fathers defended this against those who denied it.
Literally “he takes hold of”, as one grips someone to save him. Many of the Fathers and the Latin Vulgate understood it as “he took on” our nature, and the Malayalam POC follows that sense.
to make a sacrifice of atonement
The verb is linked with the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16). Christ himself takes away what separates the people from God.
vv: Since, therefore, the children share flesh and blood, he himself likewise shared the same things, so that through death he might destroy the one who has the power of death, that is, the devil,
He does not fight death from outside. He goes into it. Today's feast shows the first step on that road: a child whose flesh and blood are carried to the Temple, already offered.
and free those who all their lives were held in slavery by the fear of death.
Fear of death rules much of human life. Simeon in today's Gospel is the living picture of the opposite, an old man at peace with the thought of dying.
Because he himself was tested by what he suffered, he is able to help those who are being tested.
He does not help from a distance. The one who stands before God for us knows what weakness is like from the inside.
ch: The Catechism quotes these verses when it teaches that Christ, the Author of life, destroyed by his death the one who had the power of death (CCC 635). The Second Vatican Council says that by his incarnation the Son of God has united himself in some fashion with every human being, working with human hands and loving with a human heart (Gaudium et Spes 22). Today's Mass begins with candles carried into the church. The light that came into our darkness, in our own flesh, is what this passage describes.

r.h: Lift up your heads, O gates
set: Psalm 24 is a psalm for entering the sanctuary. It asks who may go up the hill of the Lord (24:3), and these closing verses are the answer of the procession at the gates. Many scholars think it was sung when the ark, the sign of God's presence, was carried into Jerusalem or into the Temple (compare 2 Samuel 6). In the Greek and Latin numbering it is Psalm 23.
str: v. 7: the command to the gates.
v. 8: the question, and the answer: the Lord, mighty in battle.
vv. 9–10: the same command and question repeated, with the fuller answer: the Lord of hosts.
kw: The city gates are addressed as if they were people who must lift their heads. Those ancient doors are told, in effect, that they are too small for the one who is coming.
Kābôd, glory, is literally weight or importance. In the Bible it is the visible presence of God, the glory that filled the tent and the Temple (Exodus 40:34; 1 Kings 8:11).
The Lord of all the armies of heaven, and the title linked with the ark (1 Samuel 4:4). The same title closes the first verse of today's Malachi.
vv: Lift up your heads, O gates! and be lifted up, O ancient doors! that the King of glory may come in.
On this feast the words become gently ironic. The gates of the Temple do not lift themselves, and no one in the courts turns to look. Yet the King really is coming in, in his mother's arms.
Who is the King of glory? The Lord, strong and mighty, the Lord, mighty in battle.
He has come to fight, as Hebrews says, against death itself. It will be a strange battle, won by being defeated.
Who is this King of glory? The Lord of hosts, he is the King of glory.
The question is asked twice. On this day it is answered by Simeon and by Anna.
ch: Several of the Fathers read these verses of the risen Christ going up into heaven at the Ascension (in substance), and the Eastern and Western liturgies have long used them in processions, above all at the entrance to a church. Today, as the people walk with their candles, the Church turns them to the first entrance of Christ into his Temple.

r.h: My eyes have seen your salvation
set: Forty days after the birth of a son, a Jewish mother came to the sanctuary for the rite of purification. She brought a lamb and a bird, or two birds if she could not afford a lamb (Leviticus 12:2–8). Separately, every firstborn son belonged to the Lord and was bought back with a payment (Exodus 13:2, 12–13; Numbers 18:15–16).

Luke weaves these customs into one scene. He says “their” purification, although the Law speaks only of the mother, and he mentions no payment to buy the child back. The child is simply given to God, as Hannah gave Samuel at the sanctuary (1 Samuel 1:24–28). Again and again he repeats that all this was done according to the law of the Lord. The Lord's family is a devout Jewish family, living by the Torah.
str: vv. 22–24: Mary and Joseph bring the child and the offering of the poor.
vv. 25–28: Simeon, led by the Spirit, takes the child in his arms.
vv. 29–32: his song: salvation for all peoples.
vv. 33–35: the second word: a sign opposed, and a sword for Mary.
vv. 36–38: Anna gives thanks and speaks of the child.
vv. 39–40: home to Nazareth.
¶ The shorter form of the Gospel ends with Simeon's song at v. 32.
kw: What Simeon awaits (v. 25). It recalls “Comfort, O comfort my people” (Isaiah 40:1). Anna's hearers are looking for the “redemption of Jerusalem” (v. 38), which says the same thing: Israel's hope is met in this child.

A servant's words to his owner. The verb is used of releasing someone from duty or service, and it can also mean to die. Simeon is a watchman who may at last go off duty, because what he was posted to see has come.
The same word as in the Greek of Isaiah 40:5, “all flesh shall see the salvation of God”, which Luke quotes at 3:6. Simeon has it in his arms.
a sign that will be opposed
Literally “spoken against”. The child divides people, because each one has to take a position towards him. So the “inner thoughts of many” come to light.
vv: they brought him up to Jerusalem to present him to the Lord
The word for “present” is also used of offerings. He enters the Temple as one who is given.
and they offered a sacrifice according to what is stated in the law of the Lord, “a pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons.”
This is the offering that the Law allows for those who cannot afford a lamb (Leviticus 12:8). The Lamb of God has come, and his parents do not have the price of a lamb.
Guided by the Spirit, Simeon came into the temple;
The Holy Spirit is named three times in three verses (2:25, 26, 27). Luke's Gospel opens in the Temple with the Spirit at work among Israel's faithful, before the public ministry has even begun.

“Master, now you are dismissing your servant in peace, according to your word; for my eyes have seen your salvation, which you have prepared in the presence of all peoples, a light for revelation to the Gentiles and for glory to your people Israel.”
Simeon's song draws on Isaiah 42:6 and 49:6, the servant as a light to the nations. Note the order: the light for the Gentiles is also the glory of Israel. Neither takes anything from the other.
and a sword will pierce your own soul too.
Only here, in all the Gospels, does anyone speak of Mary's sorrow in advance. The word is rhomphaia, a large sword. She hears it with the child in the arms of an old man, on a day of offering.
At that moment she came, and began to praise God and to speak about the child to all who were looking for the redemption of Jerusalem.

Anna, a prophet of the northern tribe of Asher, is an old widow who has spent her life in fasting and prayer. Luke places a woman beside a man, as he often does, and she is the first to speak of the child to others in the Temple. Her words are not given. It is enough that she told them.
ch: The Catechism says that with Simeon and Anna all Israel awaits its encounter with the Saviour, which is the name the Byzantine tradition gives to this feast. Jesus is recognized as the long-expected Messiah, the light to the nations and the glory of Israel, but also a sign that is spoken against. And the sword foretold for Mary announces Christ's perfect and unique offering on the Cross (CCC 529). The Second Vatican Council sees Mary here making the offering of the poor and hearing the prophecy of the sword, already joined with her Son in his saving work (Lumen Gentium 57). St Sophronius of Jerusalem preached on this feast: let us all hasten to meet Christ with lighted candles, carrying a sign of the light that has come (in substance). His sermon is read in the Liturgy of the Hours for this day.

qa: Why would Mary need to be purified, if she was without sin?

The purity laws of Leviticus 12 have nothing to do with sin. Childbirth is not sinful. These laws concern fitness to come to the sanctuary, after the mystery of blood and life. Mary, conceived without sin, goes there like any other Jewish mother. She does what the Law asks, as her Son will go to John to be baptized. Humility and obedience bring her to the Temple, and not any guilt.
Why do we bless candles today?

The feast is known in many places as Candlemas, from the “light for revelation to the Gentiles” in Simeon's song. In Jerusalem in the late fourth century the pilgrim Egeria described a solemn celebration of this fortieth day, and by the end of the seventh century Rome had a procession. A blessed candle is a sacramental, a sign that prepares us to receive grace (CCC 1667, 1670). It has no power of its own. It points to Christ, and it asks us to carry him.
How old was Anna?

The Greek of v. 37 can mean either that she had reached the age of eighty-four, as the NRSV and the POC take it, or that she had been a widow for eighty-four years. Either way, Luke's point is that she had given a long life to waiting on God.
rite: This feast closes the circle of Christmas, forty days after 25 December. Before the reform of the calendar in 1969 the Roman Rite called it the Purification of the Blessed Virgin Mary; it is now the Presentation of the Lord, which places Christ at the centre without losing his Mother. The Roman Missal gives a blessing of candles and a procession (or a solemn entrance) before Mass. The Canticle of Simeon, the Nunc Dimittis, is sung every night at Night Prayer. St John Paul II made this the World Day for Consecrated Life in 1997, because religious men and women, like the child in the Temple, are given to God, and, like Anna, they stay close to him. It is a good day for a parish to thank its sisters, brothers and priests.
study: Malachi says, “the Lord whom you seek.” What am I really looking for when I ask God to come into my life, and would I be ready if he came to purify it?
Only Simeon and Anna noticed who had entered the Temple. What had their long years of prayer done to prepare them? How might I learn to recognize Christ in ordinary things?
Hebrews speaks of “slavery by the fear of death”. Where does that fear rule in my life? What might Simeon's “in peace” mean for someone preparing for death?
Mary heard of the sword on a day of joy. How can a family hold joy and sorrow together in faith?

lead: Hebrews says that the hard things in a Christian life can be the training of a Father who loves us. Mark shows people who cannot receive what God gives, because they think they already know Jesus too well. In the one reading a person accepts correction and grows, and in the other people take offense and receive little. Psalm 103 gives the tone for both: “As a father has compassion for his children, so the Lord has compassion for those who fear him.”

r.h: The Lord disciplines those whom he loves
set: The letter has just called its readers to run the race with their eyes on Jesus (12:1–3). They are tired and under pressure, though they have not yet had to die for the faith (v. 4). The author now quotes Proverbs 3:11–12 to help them read what they are going through. The hard times are not a sign that God has abandoned them.
str: vv. 4–6: you have forgotten the word that calls you children.
v. 7: endure, because God is treating you as children.
v. 11: discipline hurts now and bears fruit later.
vv. 12–15: so strengthen one another, pursue peace and holiness, and watch over each other.
kw: From pais, a child. It means the whole upbringing of a child: teaching, correction and training. It is not simply punishment.
The word gives us “gymnasium”. The picture is of an athlete, and it continues the race of 12:1.
Literally “watching over”, from the family of words that gives us episkopos, bishop. Here the whole community is told to do it for one another.
vv: for the Lord disciplines those whom he loves, and chastises every child whom he accepts.

This cannot be turned into a claim that every sorrow is a punishment sent by God. Job's story forbids that. The author is speaking to believers who wonder whether God has forgotten them, and he says that God treats them as his children even here.
Now, discipline always seems painful rather than pleasant at the time, but later it yields the peaceful fruit of righteousness to those who have been trained by it.
An honest verse. It does not say that suffering feels good. “At the time” and “later” are the key words.
Pursue peace with everyone, and the holiness without which no one will see the Lord.

Peace and holiness are set side by side: a person cannot be holy alone and at war with everyone. The “root of bitterness” in v. 15 comes from Deuteronomy 29:18. One bitter person can poison a whole community.
ch: The Catechism says that illness and suffering can lead to anguish and to revolt against God, but that they can also make a person more mature and help him to see what is essential (CCC 1501). By his Passion and Death, Christ has given suffering a new meaning (CCC 1505). The call to holiness in v. 14 is for everyone in the Church, as the Second Vatican Council teaches (Lumen Gentium 40).

r.h: Is not this the carpenter?
set: Jesus has just raised the daughter of Jairus (5:35–43). He now goes home to Nazareth, a small village in the hills of Galilee, and teaches in the synagogue on the sabbath. So far in Mark, crowds have followed Jesus. Here those who know him best take offense.
str: vv. 1–2: he teaches, and they are astounded: where did he get this?
v. 3: they think they know: his work, his mother, his relatives. They take offense.
v. 4: the saying about the prophet.
vv. 5–6: few healings, and Jesus' amazement.
kw: A craftsman who worked in wood and also in stone or metal. St Justin Martyr, in the second century, says that Jesus made ploughs and yokes. The man with this wisdom works with his hands.
From skandalon, a stumbling block. What trips them up is how ordinary he is.
Here it is more than a lack of information. It is a refusal to trust the one who stands in front of them.
vv: Is not this the carpenter, the son of Mary and brother of James and Joses and Judas and Simon, and are not his sisters here with us?” And they took offense at him.

Mark nowhere mentions Mary's husband Joseph, and this is the only time he names Mary. The list of relatives is given in order to say: we know all about him. But to know where someone comes from is not to know who he is.
And he could do no deed of power there, except that he laid his hands on a few sick people and cured them.

Jesus' power has not run out. In Mark, healing goes with faith (5:34), and he does not force himself on anyone. Matthew words it gently: “he did not do many deeds of power there” (13:58). Even so, a few are healed.
And he was amazed at their unbelief.
It is rare for the Gospels to say that Jesus was amazed. Here it is at unbelief; in Luke 7:9 it is at a Gentile centurion's faith.
ch: The Church sees in the hidden years at Nazareth a part of the mystery of salvation: the Son of God earned his living by the work of his hands, and so ordinary work and family life are honoured (CCC 531–533). The Second Vatican Council says that he worked with human hands (Gaudium et Spes 22). The offense of Nazareth is still with us: it is not always easy to find God in what is familiar, in a parish, a sacrament or a neighbour.

qa: Did Jesus have brothers and sisters, if Mary remained a virgin?

The Church professes Mary's perpetual virginity, and she has always understood these “brothers” as close relatives. Hebrew and Aramaic did not have a separate common word for cousin: Lot is called Abraham's “brother” (Genesis 14:14, Hebrew text). James and Joses are named later as sons of another Mary, a disciple of Christ (Mark 15:40; CCC 500). Other Christians read the text in other ways, and a calm and respectful conversation is the best way to take up this question.
rite: Two optional memorials are offered today. St Blaise, bishop of Sebaste in Armenia, was martyred in the early fourth century. Almost everything told about him comes from later legend, including the boy he is said to have saved from choking on a fish bone, but devotion to him is old and widespread. From this comes the blessing of throats today, with two crossed candles and the prayer that through his intercession God may deliver us from every disease of the throat and from every other illness. St Ansgar (died 865), a monk of Corbie and later Archbishop of Hamburg and Bremen, is called the Apostle of the North for his mission to Denmark and Sweden. After years of discouragement, he kept working without seeing much fruit, which is a good commentary on Hebrews 12:11.
study: What difficulty in my life, which I have treated only as a misfortune, might I read as God's training of a beloved child?
Who is “the carpenter” in my life, someone so familiar that I no longer listen when God may be speaking through him or her?

lead: Hebrews describes where the Christian stands at worship: not at a mountain of fire, but in the assembly of angels and saints, in front of Jesus. Mark shows the same Jesus sending twelve men out with almost nothing, to give what they have received. We come in to the feast and we are sent out, and the two go together. Psalm 48, in praise of the city of God, supplies the words for the gathering: “We ponder your steadfast love, O God, in the midst of your temple.”

r.h: You have come to Mount Zion
set: This is one of the high points of the letter. The author sets two mountains in front of his tired readers. One is Sinai, as Exodus 19 and Deuteronomy 4–5 describe it: fire, darkness and a voice that frightened the people. The other is Zion, the heavenly city. His argument is pastoral: look at where you have come, and do not turn back. The Lectionary omits v. 20.
str: vv. 18–19, 21: you have not come to this: the terrors of Sinai.
vv. 22–24: you have come to this: a long list, from the city to the blood of Jesus.
kw: A festival assembly, the word used for a great public celebration. Only here in the New Testament. Where Sinai had dread, Zion has a feast.
Ekklēsia is the word for Church. The firstborn were the ones who belonged to God in a special way, as this week's feast of the Presentation recalled. Their names are written in heaven.
One who stands between two parties. Hebrews uses it of Jesus three times (8:6; 9:15; 12:24), always with the new covenant.
vv: Indeed, so terrifying was the sight that Moses said, “I tremble with fear.”
Exodus does not record these words at Sinai. The nearest is Deuteronomy 9:19, when Moses was afraid after the golden calf. Hebrews brings it into this scene.
But you have come to Mount Zion and to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem, and to innumerable angels in festal gathering,
The tense is striking: “you have come”. The author does not say “you will come one day”. The Christian who worships is already, in hope and in sacrament, in that company.
and to Jesus, the mediator of a new covenant, and to the sprinkled blood that speaks a better word than the blood of Abel.

The blood of Abel cried out to God from the ground (Genesis 4:10). The blood of Jesus also speaks, and it asks for mercy. The sprinkling recalls the blood with which Moses sealed the covenant (Exodus 24:8). The whole list ends here, on the note of mercy.
ch: The Second Vatican Council teaches that in the earthly liturgy we take part in a foretaste of the heavenly liturgy which is celebrated in the holy city of Jerusalem (Sacrosanctum Concilium 8; CCC 1090). This is why every Preface ends by joining the angels and saints in the Holy, Holy, Holy. At every Mass, however small the parish and however few the people, this passage is what is really happening.

r.h: He began to send them out two by two
set: After the rejection at Nazareth, the work widens. Jesus chose the Twelve “to be with him, and to be sent out” (3:14). They have been with him, and now they are sent. Mark sets their mission around the story of John's death (6:14–29). They return only at 6:30.
str: v. 7: two by two, with authority.
vv. 8–9: what to take, and it is almost nothing.
vv. 10–11: where to stay, and what to do if refused.
vv. 12–13: what they did: preached repentance, cast out demons, anointed the sick.
kw: The verb behind the word “apostle”, one who is sent with the authority of the sender. Mark will call them apostles when they return (6:30).
The authority that amazed people in Jesus' own teaching (1:22, 27). He now shares it.
Olive oil was used as a medicine in the ancient world (compare Luke 10:34). Here it is joined to the power of Jesus' mission. Only Mark mentions it in this account.
vv: He called the twelve and began to send them out two by two, and gave them authority over the unclean spirits.
Two witnesses were needed to establish a matter under the Law (Deuteronomy 19:15). Two also means company on the road. No one in the Gospel is sent to be a lone hero.
He ordered them to take nothing for their journey except a staff; no bread, no bag, no money in their belts;

The poverty of the mission is the message: they depend on God and on the people who receive them. Matthew 10:10 and Luke 9:3 report that even the staff was forbidden. The Gospel writers differ on the detail and agree on the point.
So they went out and proclaimed that all should repent. They cast out many demons, and anointed with oil many who were sick and cured them.
They say what John said (1:4) and what Jesus said (1:15). Word and healing go together, as they do in Jesus' own work.
ch: The Catechism quotes these two verses in speaking of Christ's call to his disciples to share his ministry of compassion and healing (CCC 1506). The Council of Trent taught that the sacrament of the Anointing of the Sick is alluded to by Mark and is recommended and promulgated by James (James 5:14–15; CCC 1511). The sending of the Twelve is the root of the apostolic ministry in the Church (CCC 858–859).

qa: Does Hebrews mean that Sinai was a bad thing, or that God has rejected Israel?

No. Sinai was God's own work, and the Law is holy. Hebrews compares the fear of that first meeting with the access given in Christ, and it does so in order to encourage tired Christians, not to condemn anyone. The Church teaches that the New Testament lies hidden in the Old and the Old is made clear in the New (Dei Verbum 16), and that God's covenant with Israel has never been revoked (CCC 121; Nostra Aetate 4).
study: When I go to Mass, do I see only the people around me? How would it change my prayer to remember the company that Hebrews lists?
What would I find it hardest to leave behind if Jesus sent me out with “nothing for their journey”, as he sent the Twelve? Who is the companion that he has given me for the road?

lead: Hebrews ends with plain advice: love one another, welcome strangers, remember prisoners, honour marriage, do not love money. Its reason is one great sentence: “Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever.” Mark tells a story that shows what such steadiness costs. A prophet in prison stays true, while a king on a throne, who knows better, gives way before his guests. Psalm 27 is the prayer of those who stand firm: “The Lord is my light and my salvation.” It suits St Agatha, whom the Church remembers today.

r.h: The same yesterday and today and forever
set: After the great vision of Zion, the last chapter of Hebrews turns to daily life. These short commands are what worship looks like outside the church door. The readers have known imprisonment and the loss of property (10:32–34), so the mention of prisoners and of money is not abstract.
str: vv. 1–3: love: brothers and sisters, strangers, prisoners.
vv. 4–6: marriage and money, and the promise that God will not leave us.
vv. 7–8: remember your leaders; Christ does not change.
kw: Literally love of brothers and sisters. The Christians are one family (compare 2:11).
Literally love of strangers. In Greek the word stands right after philadelphia: love for those who are near must not close the door on those who are far.
One word in Greek: “not a lover of silver”. Hebrews gives the reason in the same verse: the person who has God's promise does not need to hold on so tightly.
vv: Do not neglect to show hospitality to strangers, for by doing that some have entertained angels without knowing it.
The author is thinking of Abraham at Mamre and Lot at Sodom (Genesis 18–19). St Benedict tells his monks to welcome all guests as Christ himself (Rule 53).
Remember those who are in prison, as though you were in prison with them;
Compare Matthew 25:36. In the ancient world prisoners often depended on friends for food, and to visit them could be dangerous.
Keep your lives free from the love of money, and be content with what you have; for he has said, “I will never leave you or forsake you.”
The quotation recalls the words of Moses to Israel and God's words to Joshua (Deuteronomy 31:6; Joshua 1:5). The next verse answers with Psalm 118:6.
Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever.

Leaders die (v. 7), and circumstances change, but Christ does not. The first readers needed this as much as we do. “Yesterday” includes the Cross. “Today” is the word Hebrews has repeated from Psalm 95 (3:7–15).
ch: The Second Vatican Council quotes this verse: beneath all change there are many things which do not change, and which have their ultimate foundation in Christ, who is the same yesterday and today and forever (Gaudium et Spes 10). The Roman Rite makes it visible at the Easter Vigil, when the priest marks the Paschal candle with the words “Christ yesterday and today, the Beginning and the End”.

r.h: John, whom I beheaded
set: While the Twelve are away on mission, Mark tells this story. He sets it between their sending (6:7–13) and their return (6:30), and so the disciples learn what their mission may cost. This Herod is Herod Antipas, son of Herod the Great. He ruled Galilee and Perea under Rome from 4 BC to AD 39. Mark calls him “king” in the popular way; Matthew and Luke use the exact title, tetrarch.

The Jewish historian Josephus also tells of John's death (Antiquities 18). He says that John was held in the fortress of Machaerus, east of the Dead Sea, and that Herod feared his influence over the people. The Gospel and Josephus differ in some details, including the name of Herodias' first husband, but both remember John as a good man whom a ruler killed.
str: vv. 14–16: who is Jesus? Herod's bad conscience answers: John.
vv. 17–20: flashback: why John was in prison.
vv. 21–25: the banquet, the dance, the oath, the request.
vv. 26–28: the execution.
v. 29: John's disciples bury him.
kw: What John kept saying; the Greek tense suggests repetition. The law is Leviticus 18:16 and 20:21. John says this to the ruler's face.
Herod does not know what to do with John. He respects him, is troubled by him and likes to listen to him. He hears the truth with pleasure and still does nothing.
The word for a corpse. Mark uses it again when Joseph of Arimathea asks for the body of Jesus (15:45). The story ends as Jesus' own will end, with a body laid in a tomb by those who loved him.
vv: For John had been telling Herod, “It is not lawful for you to have your brother’s wife.”
John does not go looking for a political quarrel. He says what is true about one man's marriage, and that man has power.
When he heard him, he was greatly perplexed; and yet he liked to listen to him.
A sharp portrait. Herod is not a monster. It is possible to enjoy good preaching for years without ever being changed by it.
When his daughter Herodias came in and danced,

The manuscripts differ. Some read “his daughter Herodias”, as the NRSV does, and others read “the daughter of Herodias”, as the POC does. Mark does not name her otherwise; the name Salome comes from Josephus. The offer of “half of my kingdom” (v. 23) echoes the words of King Ahasuerus to Esther (Esther 5:3; 7:2).
The king was deeply grieved; yet out of regard for his oaths and for the guests, he did not want to refuse her.
He is afraid of losing face, and he gives way though he knows what is right. Pilate will do the same in Mark 15:15, “wishing to satisfy the crowd”.
ch: The Catechism says that John, the precursor of the Messiah, bore witness to him by his preaching, his baptism of repentance and finally his martyrdom (CCC 523). St John Paul II names him among those who would rather die than compromise with evil (Veritatis Splendor 91). St Bede the Venerable observes that John was not asked to deny Christ, but only to keep silent about the truth, and that he died for Christ who is the Truth (in substance). The Church keeps the Passion of St John the Baptist on 29 August.

qa: Should Herod have kept his oath?

No. His oath was rash, and an oath to do evil does not bind. St Thomas Aquinas teaches that to keep such an oath is a further sin (Summa Theologiae II-II, q. 89, a. 7). The name of God may not be used to cover a wrong, and the holiness of that Name is what oaths are meant to respect (CCC 2150, 2155). Herod is held by his pride and by the eyes of his guests, not by any duty to God.
rite: St Agatha is one of the women martyrs named in the Roman Canon (Eucharistic Prayer I), with Felicity, Perpetua, Lucy, Agnes, Cecilia and Anastasia. She was a young woman of Sicily, and her cult at Catania is ancient. She probably died in the persecution of the third century. The accounts of her sufferings were written long after and cannot be relied on in their details, but the Church's memory of her witness is firm. Tradition remembers her standing firm before a powerful official, and that places her beside John. Remember her when praying Hebrews 13:3 for those who suffer violence, above all women and girls, in many lands.
study: Hebrews lists several very practical things in eight verses. Which one is Christ asking of me this week?
Herod liked to listen to John, and did nothing. What word of God have I enjoyed hearing for a long time without acting on it?

lead: The shepherd joins today's readings. Hebrews closes with a blessing in the name of “the great shepherd of the sheep”. Mark sees a crowd “like sheep without a shepherd”, and Jesus, who had taken his tired apostles away to rest, gives up the rest and teaches them. Psalm 23, the shepherd psalm, is the response. In between, Hebrews tells Christians what sacrifice means in daily life, joined to Christ's one offering: praise, doing good and sharing what they have. St Paul Miki and his companions, on their crosses at Nagasaki, praised God and forgave.

r.h: The great shepherd of the sheep
set: These are the last words of the letter before its short farewell. The author has argued that Christ's sacrifice ended the need for the animal sacrifices. What, then, do Christians offer in their daily lives, through him? The answer is here, and then comes the blessing. These offerings do not replace the Eucharist, in which his one sacrifice is made present (CCC 1366); they flow from it. Hebrews does not name its author, and the Church has received it among the letters linked with St Paul.
str: vv. 15–16: the sacrifices of daily Christian life, offered through Christ: praise and sharing.
v. 17: obey your leaders, who will have to answer for you.
vv. 20–21: a solemn blessing that gathers up the letter.
kw: A phrase from the Greek Psalms and the Law (Psalm 50:14, 23; Leviticus 7:12). The “fruit of lips” comes from Hosea 14:2. Through Christ, our worship is itself an offering.
The word usually translated “fellowship”. Here it means giving material help. Hebrews calls it a sacrifice, along with praise.
To put in order, to mend. It is the word used for James and John mending their nets (Mark 1:19). God repairs what is broken in us and makes us fit for his work.
vv: Through him, then, let us continually offer a sacrifice of praise to God, that is, the fruit of lips that confess his name.
“Through him” is the key. We have nothing to offer apart from him. And the offering is “continual”, not only in church.
Do not neglect to do good and to share what you have, for such sacrifices are pleasing to God.
Worship and charity are not two different departments. The same word, “sacrifice”, covers both.
Now may the God of peace, who brought back from the dead our Lord Jesus, the great shepherd of the sheep, by the blood of the eternal covenant,

This is the only place where Hebrews speaks directly of Jesus' resurrection. Elsewhere it speaks of his being exalted to God's right hand. The words may echo Isaiah 63:11, where God brought up from the sea the shepherd of his flock, Moses. A greater one has now been brought up, from death.
ch: The Catechism lists “sacrifice of praise”, citing Hebrews 13:15, among the names of the Eucharist (CCC 1330), and the Roman Canon uses the same words. “The blood of the eternal covenant” is heard at every Mass in the words over the chalice. The Second Vatican Council quotes v. 17 when it asks the laity to obey their pastors willingly, and to pray for them, so that they may do their work with joy (Lumen Gentium 37). The same passage asks pastors to recognize and promote the dignity of the laity.

r.h: Like sheep without a shepherd
set: The Twelve come back from the mission on which they were sent at 6:7. Mark has told of John's death in the meantime, so they return into a darker world. This is the only certain place where Mark calls them “apostles”, because they have just done what the word means. The passage leads straight into the feeding of the five thousand (6:35–44), which the Lectionary does not read today.
str: v. 30: the apostles report.
v. 31: Jesus invites them to rest.
vv. 32–33: they go by boat, and the crowd gets there first on foot.
v. 34: Jesus sees them, has compassion, and teaches.
kw: Jesus says this to tired workers. The same root stands behind “I will give you rest” in Matthew 11:28.
The word for wilderness, the place of the Exodus, where God fed Israel. Mark uses it for Jesus' own prayer (1:35).

From the word for one's inner organs: he was moved in the depths. In the Gospels it is used only of Jesus and of characters in his parables, such as the Good Samaritan and the father of the prodigal son.
vv: He said to them, “Come away to a deserted place all by yourselves and rest a while.” For many were coming and going, and they had no leisure even to eat.
Jesus cares about tired people, including those who work for him. It is not selfish to rest. Anyone in ministry may take this verse as a command.
Now many saw them going and recognized them, and they hurried there on foot from all the towns and arrived ahead of them.
No plan survives the people's hunger. It is rather touching: they run round the lake to be there when he lands.
As he went ashore, he saw a great crowd; and he had compassion for them, because they were like sheep without a shepherd; and he began to teach them many things.

Moses asked God for a leader so that Israel would not be “like sheep without a shepherd” (Numbers 27:17), and Ezekiel 34 promised that God himself would be their shepherd. Jesus does not show annoyance at losing his rest. And the first thing he gives is teaching, before any bread.
ch: The Catechism says that the Church is a sheepfold whose one and necessary door is Christ, and that her sheep are led and nourished by Christ himself, the Good Shepherd and Prince of shepherds, who gave his life for them (CCC 754; Lumen Gentium 6). Every pastor in the Church shares in that compassion, and every priest, catechist and parent learns from this passage both the need to rest and the readiness to give up rest for someone in need.

qa: Jesus told them to rest, but then he did not let them. So which does he want?

Both. He wants his friends to rest, and the Church teaches that human life has a rhythm of work and rest (CCC 2184). The Gospel also shows what love does when a need arises that cannot wait. A person who never rests soon has nothing to give. A person who never gives up his rest has not learned from the Shepherd. Mark also shows Jesus going off alone to pray after this same day (6:46).
rite: St Paul Miki, a Japanese Jesuit not yet ordained priest, was crucified on a hill at Nagasaki on 5 February 1597 with twenty-five companions: Jesuits, Franciscans and lay Japanese Christians, among them boys. An account of the time reports that he preached from the cross and forgave those who had condemned him. They were canonized in 1862. When missionaries returned to Japan in the nineteenth century, they found communities near Nagasaki who had kept the faith for over two hundred years without priests. They were sheep without a shepherd in one sense, and yet the great Shepherd had not left them. This is a good day to pray for the Church in Asia.
study: Hebrews names three kinds of sacrifice: praise, doing good and sharing. Which of these is missing from my week?
When have my plans for rest been interrupted by someone in need? How did I respond? And when do I need to hear “Come away … and rest a while”?

lead: This Sunday begins in the middle of the night, with Job awake and in pain, counting the hours until dawn. It ends before dawn, with Jesus up and praying in a deserted place. In between, the Psalm answers Job from afar: the God who numbers the stars also bandages a wound. In Mark's Gospel, a woman in bed with a fever is taken by the hand and lifted up, and she begins to serve. Paul, in his turn, has made himself a servant of all, because the good news is too great to keep. So the movement of the day runs from night to healing to mission. Those who are healed are sent.

r.h: Nights of misery
set: The Book of Job is one of the great works of the Bible's wisdom tradition, and it cannot be dated with certainty. Its hero is not an Israelite but a man from the land of Uz (1:1). In the prose opening he loses his children, his wealth and his health, and he is not told why. Friends arrive and, after long silence, explain that suffering must be the result of sin. Job refuses this answer.
Chapters 6–7 are his reply to the first friend, Eliphaz. In chapter 7 he turns to speak to God directly. The Lectionary leaves out v. 5, with its description of his sores.
str: vv. 1–2: human life compared with hard service: the soldier, the slave, the hired hand.
vv. 3–4: Job's own months and nights.
vv. 6–7: days that run out without hope; and then a prayer: remember.
kw: Usually military service: the word behind “hosts” in “Lord of hosts”. Isaiah 40:2 uses it of Jerusalem's term of hardship. Life feels like conscription, something a person never chose and cannot leave.
Šāw’ means emptiness or futility. A hired man at least gets his wages at evening. Job's pay is months of nothing.
This word can also mean a cord or thread (Joshua 2:18, 21). Coming right after the weaver's shuttle, it makes a sad play on words: Job's days run out “without thread” and “without hope” at once.
vv: “Do not human beings have a hard service on earth, and are not their days like the days of a laborer?
Job starts with everybody, and he speaks for all who work with no rest and no reward. Then, in v. 3, he comes to himself.
When I lie down I say, ‘When shall I rise?’ But the night is long, and I am full of tossing until dawn.
Anyone who has sat by a sick bed, or has been in one, knows this verse. Scripture does not tidy it up. These words are God's word as well as Job's.
My days are swifter than a weaver’s shuttle, and come to their end without hope.
The odd thing is that the nights are long and the days are short. That is exactly how suffering feels.
“Remember that my life is a breath; my eye will never again see good.
The verb is singular and addressed to God. Job's despair has turned into a prayer. Even a person who thinks he will never see good again may still say “Remember” to God.
ch: St John Paul II takes Job as the Old Testament's proof that not all suffering is a punishment for sin, even though Job's friends thought so (Salvifici Doloris 11). The Catechism adds that no quick answer will do for the question of evil, and that the whole of the Christian message is the answer to it (CCC 309). St Gregory the Great wrote his long Moralia on this book and read Job as a figure of Christ (in substance). In the older Office of the Dead the Church read from Job, including from this very chapter. She gives the sufferer his words, because he has a right to them.

r.h: He heals the brokenhearted
set: Psalms 146–150 close the Psalter with one long Hallelujah. Psalm 147 speaks of God building up Jerusalem and gathering the outcasts (v. 2), and many scholars therefore place it after the return from exile. In the Greek and Latin numbering these verses belong to Psalm 146. The Psalm comes as an answer to Job: not an explanation, but a description of who God is.
str: vv. 1–2: a call to praise, and the reason: he builds and gathers.
vv. 3–4: he heals the wounded and names the stars.
vv. 5–6: his greatness, and what he does with it: he lifts up the lowly.
kw: Literally “broken of heart”. A similar phrase stands in Psalm 34:18. In the Old Testament the heart is the centre of the person, not just of the feelings.
The word for tying on a dressing. The same verb appears in Isaiah 61:1, “to bind up the brokenhearted”.
The lowly, the poor who have no one but God. The Beatitude of the meek (Matthew 5:5) comes from the same idea, through Psalm 37:11.
vv: He heals the brokenhearted, and binds up their wounds.
Put this next to Job 7. The Psalm does not explain why the wound came. It tells us who kneels down beside it.
He determines the number of the stars; he gives to all of them their names.
The two verses are set together on purpose. The one who has the vast sky in order has the time to bandage a wound. Compare Genesis 15:5.
The Lord lifts up the downtrodden; he casts the wicked to the ground.
“Lifts up” prepares us for Mark, where Jesus lifts up a sick woman by the hand.
ch: The Catechism calls the Psalter the book in which the Word of God becomes the prayer of human beings (CCC 2587), and says that the Psalms mirror both God's great deeds and the experience of the one who prays (CCC 2588). The Church prays Psalm 147 in the Liturgy of the Hours. Today it stands as a promise that Christ fulfils in the Gospel, where his healing begins in a family's home.

r.h: Woe to me if I do not proclaim the gospel
set: In chapters 8–10 Paul is answering a question that divided the Christians of Corinth: may a believer eat meat that has been offered to idols? His answer is that love may give up a right for the sake of a weaker brother or sister. In chapter 9 he gives his own example. As an apostle he has a right to be supported by the Church, and he mentions that Cephas and others take a wife with them on their travels (9:5). But he himself has given up that right. He works with his hands (Acts 18:3) and takes no pay from the Corinthians. The Lectionary omits vv. 20–21, where he speaks of living with Jews and with those outside the Law.
str: v. 16: preaching is not a boast but a necessity.
vv. 17–18: so what is his reward? To give it away.
v. 19: bound to no one, and a slave to all.
vv. 22–23: all things to all people, for the sake of the gospel.
kw: Necessity, compulsion. This life was laid on Paul on the Damascus road; he did not choose it for himself (Acts 9:15; Galatians 1:15–16). That is why he cannot boast.
Only here in the New Testament. Paul's whole reward is to take no reward. The gift is passed on in the same way as it was received.
A word from the world of trade: to gain or to make a profit. Paul is working for a different profit. It is used five times in vv. 19–22.
A partner. Paul does not stand outside the gospel, handing it to others. He needs it too.
vv: If I proclaim the gospel, this gives me no ground for boasting, for an obligation is laid on me, and woe to me if I do not proclaim the gospel!
“Woe” is the prophets' word. Paul speaks like Jeremiah, who could not hold the word in (Jeremiah 20:9).
What then is my reward? Just this: that in my proclamation I may make the gospel free of charge,
He was paid in joy. His refusal of pay meant that no one could say he preached for money, and the poorest could hear him as easily as the rich.
For though I am free with respect to all, I have made myself a slave to all, so that I might win more of them.
This is the pattern of Christ himself, who took the form of a slave (Philippians 2:7). In a slave-owning city, these words were not a pretty metaphor.
To the weak I became weak, so that I might win the weak. I have become all things to all people, that I might by all means save some.
He does not say “all”, but “some”. It is honest. The missionary does not expect to convert the world by himself. And this is the mission's measure: it starts from the one who is weak.
ch: The Second Vatican Council makes Paul's words the Church's own: “Woe to me, if I do not preach the Gospel” (Lumen Gentium 17). St Paul VI wrote that evangelizing is the grace and vocation proper to the Church, her deepest identity: she exists in order to evangelize (Evangelii Nuntiandi 14). It belongs to every baptized person, each according to his or her place.

r.h: He took her by the hand and lifted her up
set: Last Sunday's Gospel opened Jesus' first day in Capernaum, a fishing town on the northern shore of the lake: his teaching with authority and his casting out of an unclean spirit in the synagogue (1:21–28). Today the same day goes on, from the synagogue to a house, from the house to the door at sunset, and then on to the next morning. Mark gives us one full day as a sample of the whole ministry.
Excavations at Capernaum have uncovered a house near the synagogue that early Christians venerated. Many archaeologists identify it with Peter's house, though this cannot be proved.
str: vv. 29–31: the house: the fever, the hand, the service.
vv. 32–34: the door: at sunset, the whole city.
v. 35: the deserted place: prayer before dawn.
vv. 36–38: “Everyone is searching for you.” “Let us go on.”
v. 39: throughout Galilee.
kw: The verb Mark will use for the Resurrection (16:6: “He has been raised”). Healing is already a small resurrection.

The verb that gives us “deacon”. The tense suggests continued action. Jesus will say that the Son of Man came “not to be served but to serve” (10:45), the same verb. This woman is the first human being in Mark to do what Jesus himself came to do, and women who served him are there, watching from a distance, at the Cross (15:40–41).
Jesus says that this is what he “came out” to do (v. 38). The word may simply mean leaving Capernaum, but Mark's readers may also hear more: Luke's parallel says “I was sent” (Luke 4:43).
in the morning, while it was still very dark
Three time-words in Greek. Mark will use similar words for the women coming to the tomb on Easter morning (16:2).
vv: Now Simon’s mother-in-law was in bed with a fever, and they told him about her at once.
A fever at that time could easily be fatal. And notice what the disciples do: they simply tell him. This is intercession at its simplest.
He came and took her by the hand and lifted her up. Then the fever left her, and she began to serve them.
Three things happen, and Jesus says nothing. Her service is not a sign of being a servant by position; it is the response of one who has been healed.
That evening, at sunset, they brought to him all who were sick or possessed with demons.
Mark gives the time twice, “evening” and “sunset”, because the sabbath ended at sundown. Only then could people carry the sick through the town.
and he would not permit the demons to speak, because they knew him.
The demons know his name but do not love him. Jesus does not want witness from them, and his identity is to be understood only at the Cross (15:39).
In the morning, while it was still very dark, he got up and went out to a deserted place, and there he prayed.
After the busiest day, the first thing he does is pray. Mark shows Jesus at prayer alone only three times, each at night and each at a moment of pressure (1:35; 6:46; 14:32–39).
He answered, “Let us go on to the neighboring towns, so that I may proclaim the message there also; for that is what I came out to do.”
“Everyone is searching for you” sounds like success. Jesus does not stay where he is wanted. Prayer has made him clear about what he was sent for.
ch: The Catechism says that Christ's compassion toward the sick and his many healings are a clear sign that “God has visited his people” (CCC 1503), and that Jesus often draws apart to pray in solitude, on a mountain and preferably at night (CCC 2602). St Jerome, preaching on this passage, prays that the Lord may come to our house and touch our hand, so that the fever of sin may leave us and we may rise and serve (in substance). Peter's house can stand as a picture of the Church: the Lord comes in, and those who are healed begin to serve.

qa: Was Job wrong to complain to God like this?

No. At the end of the book God says that Job has spoken of him what is right, while the friends who defended God with neat explanations have not (42:7). Job comes to see that he has spoken of things too great for him (42:3), but he is never condemned for bringing his pain to God. The Psalms of lament teach the same. Honest complaint addressed to God is still prayer.
Peter had a wife. Why then are Latin priests unmarried?

The Gospel takes Peter's marriage for granted, and Paul mentions it as well (1 Corinthians 9:5). Celibacy is a discipline of the Church, not a command of Scripture. In the Latin Church priests are normally chosen from among men who live in celibacy “for the sake of the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 19:12). In many Eastern Churches, married men may be ordained priests, and such priests are held in great respect (CCC 1579–1580). Both are honoured by the Church.
When Paul says “all things to all people”, does he mean changing the message to please people?

No. In Galatians 1:10 he says that if he were still pleasing people he would not be a servant of Christ. He changes his habits, not the gospel: he gives up his rights, his food and his comfort for others. St Augustine says that Paul became all things to all not by the cunning of a liar but by the love of one who feels with others (in substance).
rite: This is the last Sunday before Lent: Ash Wednesday falls on 10 February. On Thursday, 11 February, the Church keeps Our Lady of Lourdes and the World Day of the Sick, begun by St John Paul II in 1992. Today's readings fit that day well. A parish may use this Sunday to name its sick in the Prayer of the Faithful, to prepare those who bring Holy Communion to the homebound, and to remind people that the Anointing of the Sick is not only for the dying (CCC 1514). Like Simon's friends, we can tell Jesus about them at once.
study: Job says “Remember” to God in the middle of his despair. What would my own honest prayer sound like on a bad night?
Psalm 147 places the stars next to the wound. How does it help me to see God as both great and close? Whose wound can I help to bind up this week?
Paul says that he cannot not preach. Where and to whom has Christ given me the chance to speak of him, and what right might I give up for it?
Simon's mother-in-law rose and served. What healing have I received? What service should come from it? Before Lent begins, when will I find my “deserted place” for prayer?

lead: In the last days before Lent the Church opens the first page of the Bible and, beside it, a short scene from Mark. Genesis shows God bringing order out of darkness by his word alone. Mark shows crowds running through the villages with their sick, begging only to touch the edge of a cloak. The psalm gives the response of a creature who looks at all this and says, “Bless the Lord, O my soul.” The God who said “Let there be light” has come near enough to be touched.

r.h: And there was light
set: This is the opening of the whole Bible, and the Lectionary divides the account: today the first four days, tomorrow the rest. Many scholars think this page received its final form among Israel's priests around the time of the exile in Babylon, in the sixth century BC. The Babylonians had their own stories of creation, in which the world came out of a war among the gods, and they honoured the sun, moon and stars as divine. Genesis tells a different story: one God, no battle, and a world that is good.

The writer uses the picture of the world known in his day, with a dome overhead and waters above and below it. The Church does not read this page as a lesson in astronomy. It teaches, in the form of a solemn hymn, who made the world and what the world is for (Dei Verbum 11–12).
str: vv. 1–2: the beginning: earth without form, darkness, the deep.
vv. 3–5: day one: light, separated from darkness.
vv. 6–8: day two: the dome, separating the waters.
vv. 9–13: day three: dry land and seas, then plants.
vv. 14–19: day four: the lights in the dome.

¶ The days have a pattern. The first three make spaces, and the next three fill them: the lights on day four belong to the light of day one. Each day has the same refrain: God said, it was so, God saw, evening and morning.
kw: In the Old Testament this verb has only God as its subject. It never mentions any material or tool, so it suits an act that belongs to God alone.
A rhyming Hebrew phrase for what is empty and without shape. God's first work is not to destroy this chaos but to bring it into order.

One word for all three. The NRSV says “a wind from God”; the POC says God's chaitanyam, and many Christian readers have heard the Holy Spirit here. Both readings keep what matters: God's own power is moving over the waters.
Said four times in today's reading and seven times in the chapter. It means both good and beautiful, as a thing is when it fits its purpose.
vv: Then God said, “Let there be light”; and there was light.
No struggle and no effort. God speaks and it is. St John begins his Gospel with the same words, “In the beginning”, and calls this creating Word a person.
And God saw that the light was good; and God separated the light from the darkness.
God does not call the darkness good, but he gives it a limit and a name (v. 5). Nothing in the world stands outside his rule, not even the night.
God made the two great lights

Genesis does not use the usual words for sun and moon here, only “the greater light” and “the lesser light”. Many scholars think the writer chose this on purpose: to neighbouring peoples these were gods, and here they are lamps hung up to mark the seasons.
ch: The Catechism says that Scripture presents the Creator's work “symbolically as a succession of six days” (CCC 337), and draws from it that nothing exists that does not owe its existence to God, and that each creature has its own goodness (CCC 338–339). The Church confesses that creation is the common work of the Father, the Word and the Spirit (CCC 290–292). She proclaims this same page at the Easter Vigil, by the light of the paschal candle, because the Resurrection of Christ is the beginning of a new creation.

r.h: Even the fringe of his cloak
set: This is one of Mark's summary passages, in which he sums up many days in a few lines. It comes straight after Jesus walks on the water, a scene that ends with the disciples unable to understand, “for their hearts were hardened” (6:52). Gennesaret is the fertile plain on the north-western shore of the Sea of Galilee. They had set out for Bethsaida (6:45) but land here, and the crowds find them at once.
str: v. 53: landing at Gennesaret.
vv. 54–55: people recognize him and run to fetch the sick.
v. 56: villages, cities and farms; the sick laid in the marketplaces; all who touch him are healed.
kw: The edge of a garment, and perhaps the tassels that the Law told Israelites to wear on their clothes (Numbers 15:38). So Jesus is seen here as a faithful Jew in the dress of his people.
Mark's verb at the end of v. 56 is the ordinary word for “save”. The NRSV rightly says “healed”, but the Greek hints at more than bodily cure.
vv: When they got out of the boat, people at once recognized him,

The disciples in the boat have just failed to understand him, and the people on the shore know him immediately. They do not yet know the whole truth about him, but they know where to bring their pain.
and rushed about that whole region and began to bring the sick on mats to wherever they heard he was.
A whole district on the move, carrying those who cannot walk. The healing depends in part on the people who do the carrying.
and begged him that they might touch even the fringe of his cloak; and all who touched it were healed.

They have probably heard of the woman who was healed by touching his cloak (5:27–29). There is no magic in the cloth. The power is his, and the touch is an act of faith that even a person with no words can make.
ch: The Catechism draws a line from this scene to the sacraments: the sick try to touch Jesus, and in the sacraments Christ continues to “touch” us in order to heal us (CCC 1504). The Word of creation has taken flesh, so God's power can now reach us through what is seen and touched: water, oil, bread, a hand laid on the head.

qa: Does Genesis 1 contradict science?

No. Genesis teaches that the world comes from God and is good; it does not teach how many years creation took or how the sky is built. St Augustine warned Christians not to speak foolishly on natural matters in the name of Scripture (in substance). The Catechism welcomes scientific study of origins (CCC 283) and says that there can never be a real conflict between faith and reason, since the same God gives both (CCC 159). The order of the days serves the message: that is why there is light on the first day and a sun only on the fourth.
study: The people of Gennesaret carried their sick to Jesus. Whom could you bring to him this Lent, by prayer or by going with them?
What in your own day would change if you looked at the created world and said with God, “it is good”?

lead: Tomorrow is Ash Wednesday, and today's readings prepare the ground. Genesis tells us who we are: creatures in God's image, given the world to care for, and invited into his rest. Psalm 8 is astonished at this: “what are human beings that you are mindful of them?” Mark then shows how that dignity can be forgotten, when an honest religious practice is used to avoid honouring one's own father and mother. Lent will ask the same thing of us: is our worship a matter of the lips or of the heart?

r.h: In the image of God
set: The account begun on Monday reaches its summit. Days five and six fill the waters, the air and the land, and the sentence “Let us make” marks something new. The reading ends halfway through 2:4, where this first account of creation closes; the second account, with the garden, begins there. The two were placed side by side, and they answer different questions.
str: 1:20–23: day five: sea creatures and birds, and the first blessing.
1:24–25: day six: land animals.
1:26–31: day six: humankind in God's image, blessed and given the plants for food; “very good”.
2:1–3: day seven: God rests, blesses and hallows the day.
2:4a: closing line.
¶ The verb bārā’ appears three times in 1:27 alone, as if the writer cannot say it enough. The seventh day has no “evening and morning”.
kw: An ṣelem was a statue or figure; kings in the ancient world set up images of themselves to mark their rule. Genesis gives this role to every human being, not to the king alone: each one stands in the world as God's representative.
Here a collective word, not yet a personal name. So the next words can say “male and female he created them”. Both together, and equally, are in God's image.
A royal word. It belongs with the image: a king in God's image should rule as God does, with care. It gives no licence to destroy.
The root of the word Sabbath. God is not tired. He stops because the work is complete, and he invites his creatures to share what is finished.
vv: Then God said, “Let us make humankind in our image, according to our likeness;

Why “us”? The Hebrew leaves this open. Many scholars think of God speaking with his heavenly court or of a solemn plural of deliberation. Many Fathers, reading with the whole Bible in hand, heard a first hint of the Trinity. The one is a reading of the Hebrew, the other a reading in the light of Christ.
So God created humankind in his image, in the image of God he created them; male and female he created them.
This is the root of Christian teaching on the dignity of every person: not earned, not lost by sickness, age or poverty.
God saw everything that he had made, and indeed, it was very good.
After six times “good”, now “very good”, said of the whole, with humankind in it.
And on the seventh day God finished the work that he had done, and he rested on the seventh day from all the work that he had done.
St Augustine ends his Confessions on this verse: the seventh day has no evening, because God himself will be our rest (in substance).
ch: The Catechism says that the human being alone in creation is able to know and love his Creator, and is the only creature God has willed for its own sake (CCC 356, quoting Gaudium et Spes 24). Being in God's image means being a person, not merely something (CCC 357). Man and woman are stewards of the earth (CCC 373); Pope Francis insists that being made in God's image gives no justification for absolute domination over other creatures (Laudato Si' 67). Christ himself is “the image of the invisible God” (Colossians 1:15), and in him that image, damaged by sin, is restored (CCC 1701). The Sabbath rest finds its fulfilment for Christians in Sunday (CCC 2175).

r.h: Lips and heart
set: Pharisees and scribes from Jerusalem question Jesus about the disciples' eating habits. The Pharisees were a respected lay movement who wanted holiness to reach everyday life, and they applied to ordinary meals some of the washing rules that the Law set for priests. Their concern was a serious one. Mark explains these customs for Gentile readers who do not know them (vv. 3–4); his phrase “all the Jews” is a broad description, and scholars discuss how widely these customs were kept in that period.

This is an argument inside the Jewish family, about how best to honour God. Jesus' sharp words are for the behaviour he describes, in the people he is addressing. They are no judgement on the Jewish people (Nostra Aetate 4; CCC 575 notes that his relations with the Pharisees were not only polemical).
str: vv. 1–5: the question about unwashed hands.
vv. 6–8: Jesus answers with Isaiah 29:13: lips and heart.
vv. 9–13: a concrete example: Corban.
¶ The word “tradition” comes five times. Note the shift: “of the elders” (vv. 3, 5), then “human” (v. 8), then “your” (vv. 9, 13).
kw: Literally what is handed on. In itself the word is good: Paul uses it for what he hands on to his churches (1 Corinthians 11:2). The question is whether a tradition serves the word of God or replaces it.

An Aramaic and Hebrew word for what is offered to God. Mark translates it. The case describes someone who declares his goods dedicated, so that his parents cannot be helped from them. Later Jewish teachers themselves provided for releasing such vows for the sake of honouring parents (the Mishnah, tractate Nedarim), so the practice Jesus attacks was not the whole of Jewish teaching.
In ordinary Greek, an actor on a stage. Jesus uses it of religion that is performed. It remains a warning for every believer, in every age.
vv: ‘This people honors me with their lips, but their hearts are far from me;
Jesus takes these words from the prophet Isaiah, who spoke them to his own people. The prophets' language of self-criticism is one of the great gifts of Israel to the world.
You abandon the commandment of God and hold to human tradition.”
This sentence is the heart of the reading.
then you no longer permit doing anything for a father or mother,
The argument is very practical. An act that looks like piety towards God is being used to escape from the fourth commandment. Elderly parents go hungry, and the conscience stays quiet.
thus making void the word of God through your tradition that you have handed on.
“Making void” is a legal word: to cancel, to annul. The word of God can be cancelled by people who are very devout.
ch: The Catechism says that Jesus had to confront certain human traditions of the Pharisees that were making void the word of God (CCC 581). It also distinguishes the apostolic Tradition, which comes from Christ through the apostles, from the various theological, disciplinary, liturgical or devotional traditions, which the Church can keep, change or drop under her Magisterium (CCC 83). So this passage is no argument against Tradition as such. Scripture and Tradition flow from the same divine source (Dei Verbum 9). Grown children's duty of material and moral support to aged parents remains a serious duty (CCC 2218).

qa: Does this Gospel mean that Catholic traditions are only human rules?

No. Jesus does not reject tradition but a practice that sets aside God's command. The Church's apostolic Tradition hands on what Christ gave (CCC 78, 83). But the warning touches us too: a devotion, a custom or a parish way of doing things can be kept with great care while the poor or our own parents are forgotten. The test is the one Jesus gives: does it bring the heart near to God?
study: Is there a religious habit in your life that has become a way of avoiding something God is plainly asking?
How does your family care for its elderly members? What would honouring them mean this Lent?

lead: Lent opens with a summons and a warning. Joel calls the whole people to fast and weep, and says that God wants the heart torn open, not the clothes. Psalm 51 gives us the words for it. Paul begs the Corinthians, “be reconciled to God”, and says that the time for this is now. Then Jesus, in the Gospel, sends us into our rooms: give, pray and fast where only the Father sees.

The readings seem to pull in two directions. Joel says, “Blow the trumpet”; Jesus says, “do not sound a trumpet”. Joel gathers everyone in public; Jesus says, “shut the door”. Both are true. The Church repents together and aloud, and each person must repent alone and in earnest. On a day when we go up in public to receive ashes, the Gospel asks what is going on underneath. The key words are return, now and in secret.

r.h: Rend your hearts
set: We know little about the prophet Joel. His book gives no king and no date. Since it speaks of the temple, priests and elders but of no king, many scholars place it after the return from exile, though this is not certain. A terrible plague of locusts has stripped the land (chapter 1), and there is no grain or wine left to offer in the temple. Joel sees in this disaster a sign of “the day of the Lord” (2:1) and a call to conversion.
The reading begins with the word “even now”. Even at this late hour, when everything seems lost, the door is open.
str: vv. 12–13: God's own call: return with all your heart; rend your hearts; he is merciful.
v. 14: “Who knows?”: hope, without presuming.
vv. 15–16: the whole community is called together, from infants to the newly married.
v. 17: the priests' prayer between the porch and the altar.
v. 18: the turning point: the Lord has pity.
kw: The Old Testament's great word for conversion. It is a word of movement. You have been walking away, and now you turn around and walk home. The same root is used when v. 14 says that God may “turn”.

Tearing one's clothes was a public sign of grief (Genesis 37:34). Joel keeps the verb and changes the object. He does not forbid the outward sign, since he himself calls for a public fast; he says that the sign must be true.

This echoes God's words about himself to Moses after the golden calf (Exodus 34:6). Raḥûm is related to the Hebrew word for the womb. This is the reason for returning: not what we have done but who God is.
Love that stays faithful to a covenant, even when the other side has failed. The word comes back in today's psalm.
vv: Yet even now, says the Lord, return to me with all your heart, with fasting, with weeping, and with mourning;
“With all your heart” does not make the fasting unnecessary. Joel keeps both. The body takes part in the turning of the heart.
rend your hearts and not your clothing.
This is the most quoted line in Joel, and it is the Church's opening word for Lent.
