Who knows whether he will not turn and relent,

A beautifully modest sentence. Joel does not bargain and does not claim to control God's answer. The king of Nineveh says the same “Who knows?” in Jonah 3:9. Repentance is a hope, and not a transaction.
Let the bridegroom leave his room, and the bride her canopy.
Even the newly married, who would normally be excused from duty, must come. No one is too young, too old or too happy for this.
Between the vestibule and the altar let the priests, the ministers of the Lord, weep.

The priests stand in the place where they usually offer sacrifice and have nothing to offer, because of the locusts. They offer tears. Their appeal rests on God's own honour: why should the nations say, “Where is their God?”
Then the Lord became jealous for his land, and had pity on his people.
Here the whole book turns. God's “jealousy” is his burning love for what is his: he cannot bear to see his land in this state.
ch: The Catechism says that Jesus' call to conversion, like that of the prophets, “does not aim first at outward works”, “sackcloth and ashes”, but at conversion of the heart; without it such penances remain sterile and false. Yet interior conversion urges expression in visible signs (CCC 1430, citing Joel 2:12–13 and today's Gospel). Interior penance is a radical turning of the whole life (CCC 1431), and it is God who gives the new heart (CCC 1432). So the Church places this reading at the door of Lent every year: the ashes on the head are worth nothing without the tear in the heart, and the tear in the heart looks for a sign.

r.h: Create in me a clean heart
set: The Psalm's Hebrew title connects it with David after the prophet Nathan confronted him about Bathsheba and Uriah (2 Samuel 11–12). Many scholars think its present form comes from a later time, and its last verses suggest the exile; still, the title has taught generations of believers to pray it as the prayer of a great sinner who was forgiven. It is called the Miserere after its first word in Latin. The Church prays it at Morning Prayer on Fridays and has used it as her chief penitential psalm.
str: vv. 1–2: a cry for mercy, with three words for sin and three for forgiveness.
vv. 3–4: confession without excuses.
vv. 10–12: the prayer for a new creation.
v. 15: lips opened in praise.
kw: have mercy, steadfast love, abundant mercy
Three words for God's love in the first verse. The psalmist starts with God's mercy rather than with his own sin.
The verb of Genesis 1, used only of God. A clean heart cannot be repaired by effort. It has to be created, as the world was.

Three times in vv. 10–12: a new and right spirit, your holy spirit, a willing spirit. Verse 11 is one of the very few places in the Old Testament to say “holy spirit”. Christians read it in the light of Pentecost.
vv: Have mercy on me, O God, according to your steadfast love;
The whole appeal rests on God's character, and the psalmist offers no merits.
Against you, you alone, have I sinned, and done what is evil in your sight,
He has also wronged other people, and very seriously, if the title is to be followed. But he has seen what lies under every sin: it wounds love of God.
Create in me a clean heart, O God, and put a new and right spirit within me.
Compare Joel: there the heart must be rent, here it must be created new. God asks for what only he can give.
O Lord, open my lips, and my mouth will declare your praise.
The Church opens the Liturgy of the Hours with this verse each day. A forgiven sinner begins to sing.
ch: The Catechism quotes this psalm when it defines sin as an offence against God (CCC 431, 1850). It takes up “a broken and contrite heart” as the true spirit of worship and of conversion, which is itself the work of grace (CCC 1428, 2100). It is the natural prayer of the sacrament of Reconciliation and a fitting psalm for receiving ashes.

r.h: Now is the acceptable time
set: Paul's relations with the Christians of Corinth had been painful. In this letter he defends his ministry, and in chapter 5 he explains what it is: God has reconciled the world to himself in Christ and has given “the ministry of reconciliation” (5:18). The reading picks up at the moment when the explanation becomes a direct appeal.
str: 5:20: we are ambassadors; God appeals through us: be reconciled.
5:21: the ground for the appeal: what God did in Christ.
6:1: do not receive grace in vain.
6:2: Isaiah 49:8: and the “now” of salvation.
kw: An envoy does not speak for himself. He carries the words of the one who sent him. So the Apostle says that it is God himself who is pleading here.
The verb comes from the language of ordinary relationships, for making enemies into friends again. Note who takes the first step. God is the offended party, and God is the one who pleads.
Not time on the clock but a moment that has come and must be seized. Paul follows Isaiah's word with his own “now”, twice.
vv: So we are ambassadors for Christ, since God is making his appeal through us; we entreat you on behalf of Christ, be reconciled to God.
Paul is writing to people who are already baptized. Reconciliation is not done once and forgotten. This is why it is read to the Church on Ash Wednesday.
For our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God.

A daring verse. Christ did not become a sinner and did not sin. In the Old Testament the Hebrew word for sin can also mean a sin offering, and many Fathers and commentators hear this here. The Catechism says that Jesus “did not experience reprobation as if he himself had sinned”, but in love he stood with sinners in their distance from God (CCC 603). An exchange is taking place: he takes our place, and we are given his.
As we work together with him, we urge you also not to accept the grace of God in vain.
Grace can be received and left unused, like a letter never opened.
See, now is the acceptable time; see, now is the day of salvation!
Isaiah's “day of salvation” was a promise for a future moment. Paul says that it has arrived: it is the time in which he and his hearers are living. The liturgy says the same today.
ch: The Catechism quotes “be reconciled to God” when it names this sacrament the sacrament of Reconciliation (CCC 1424), and teaches that the bishops and priests carry on this “ministry of reconciliation” (CCC 1442). On 5:21 it teaches that Christ, sinless, took on the state of our distance from God in love (CCC 602–603). So this reading, at the start of Lent, is a direct invitation to confession. The Church's law also asks every Catholic to confess serious sins at least once a year (CCC 1457).

r.h: Your Father who sees in secret
set: This comes from the Sermon on the Mount, and it follows Jesus' teaching on a “righteousness” greater than that of the scribes and Pharisees (5:20). He takes the three works which were at the centre of the piety of his people (see Tobit 12:8) and assumes that his disciples will do all three: “whenever you give”, “whenever you pray”, “whenever you fast”. His question is about the motive. The Lectionary leaves out vv. 7–15, which contain the Lord's Prayer, and so keeps the three-part pattern clear.

“The hypocrites” here are not a way of speaking about the Jewish people. Jesus is a Jew teaching Jewish practice, and his warning is aimed at a danger in all religion. Christians have needed it as much as anyone.
str: v. 1: the general rule: beware of doing good in order to be seen.
vv. 2–4: almsgiving.
vv. 5–6: prayer.
vv. 16–18: fasting.
¶ Each part has the same shape: when you do this, do not be like the hypocrites; “they have received their reward”; but you, do it in secret, “and your Father who sees in secret will reward you”.
kw: The NRSV says “piety” in v. 1, but the Greek word is the great word of the Sermon on the Mount: a life in right relation with God.
A term from ordinary business, used on receipts for “paid in full”. The one who wants applause gets it, and the account is closed.
The Father “is in secret” and “sees in secret”. The secret room is not a hiding place from others so much as the place where he is. This is the phrase to carry through Lent.
An actor. A person who performs for an audience.
vv: “Beware of practicing your piety before others in order to be seen by them;

Jesus has just told his disciples, “let your light shine before others” (5:16). The two sayings do not conflict. Good deeds will be seen, and the question is who gets the glory: there “your Father”, here oneself.
“So whenever you give alms, do not sound a trumpet before you,
There is no clear evidence of any such trumpet. It seems to be a vivid figure of speech: he means blowing your own trumpet.
But when you give alms, do not let your left hand know what your right hand is doing,
So secret that you do not even congratulate yourself.
But whenever you pray, go into your room and shut the door and pray to your Father who is in secret;

The “room” (tameion) was the inner storeroom, in a house without many private places. This does not cancel public worship, for Jesus himself went to the synagogue and taught us to pray “Our Father”. It teaches that public prayer must grow from a hidden relationship.
But when you fast, put oil on your head and wash your face,

Oil and washing were signs of ordinary, even festive days. Fasting should make no one else's life gloomier. Some later manuscripts add at the end of these sayings that the Father will reward you “openly”, but the older ones do not have the word, and modern Bibles leave it out.
ch: The Catechism names fasting, prayer and almsgiving as the three forms of interior penance, expressing conversion in relation to oneself, to God and to others (CCC 1434), and it says that the New Law directs these practices to the “Father who sees in secret”, in contrast with the desire to “be seen by men” (CCC 1969). St Peter Chrysologus preached that prayer, mercy and fasting are one and give life to each other: fasting is the soul of prayer, and mercy is the lifeblood of fasting (in substance). So these are not three separate tasks: what we hold back by fasting goes to the poor, and all of it goes up in prayer.

qa: If Jesus says to wash our faces when fasting, why do we walk around with ashes on our foreheads?

The Gospel is asking about motive, not forbidding every visible sign. Ashes do not announce “see how holy I am”. They say the opposite: “I am a sinner, and I am dust.” They are a public confession together with the whole Church, as Joel commands. If someone wears them with pride, this Gospel judges them. If someone is embarrassed to wear them, they may be a small act of witness.
Is Ash Wednesday a holy day of obligation?

No, it is not a holy day of obligation, though it is a day of fasting and abstinence (Code of Canon Law 1251), and many Catholics who cannot attend Mass come for the ashes. Ashes are a sacramental, not a sacrament (CCC 1667–1670). In general, abstinence binds from age 14, and fasting from age 18 to 59 (Canon 1252); those who are sick or otherwise unable are excused, and the local bishops' norms should be followed.
Doesn't “reward” make religion selfish?

The reward in this passage is not a payment for points earned. Jesus sets one reward against another: the applause of others or the Father himself. The child's joy is in being seen by the Father. As the Catechism says, our merit before God is itself a gift of his grace (CCC 2006–2008).
rite: In the Roman Rite, Lent begins today and runs until the Mass of the Lord's Supper on Holy Thursday. The ashes come from palms blessed in a previous year, and they are blessed and given after the homily, with one of two formulas: “Repent, and believe in the Gospel” (Mark 1:15) or “Remember that you are dust, and to dust you shall return” (Genesis 3:19). From this day the Alleluia is not sung until the Easter Vigil. The Second Vatican Council describes Lent as having a double character, baptismal and penitential, and asks that penance be not only interior and individual but also external and social (Sacrosanctum Concilium 109–110). In the first centuries public sinners did penance in sackcloth and ashes; by around the eleventh century the custom had spread to all the faithful, who all stand in need of the same mercy. Choose your prayer, fast and alms today, and keep them small enough to be real.
study: Joel calls for a torn heart and a public fast. Which comes more easily to you, the outward sign or the inner change? What would it take to join them?
Paul says “now”. What are you putting off with God until later?
Who would be surprised to learn what you give, or how you pray? Who is to know of your Lenten sacrifice, and why?
What will you do this Lent for each of the three: for God (prayer), for yourself (fasting), and for your neighbour (almsgiving)?

lead: On the first full day of Lent the Church puts a choice in front of us. Moses says to Israel, “Choose life.” Jesus says that the way to life passes through the Cross, and that it is walked daily. Psalm 1 draws the same two roads: the tree by the water and the chaff in the wind. Lent is not only about giving something up. It is about which way we are walking.

r.h: Choose life
set: Deuteronomy is presented as Moses' last words, spoken in the land of Moab, with the Jordan still to be crossed. Moses himself will not cross it. These verses close his final appeal. Ancient treaties ended with lists of blessings and curses and called witnesses, and Deuteronomy shapes Israel's covenant in a similar way. Other nations called on their gods as witnesses; here it is heaven and earth (v. 19), for Israel has only one God.
str: v. 15: two ways are set out: life and death.
v. 16: the first way: love, walk, keep, and live.
vv. 17–18: the second way: the heart turns away, and you perish.
vv. 19–20: witnesses and the appeal: choose life.
kw: In Deuteronomy God is the one who chooses Israel (7:6–7). Now Israel is asked to choose in return. The covenant has two partners, and the human one is really able to say yes or no.
The same verb is used of a man who “clings to his wife” (Genesis 2:24). Obedience here is more than keeping rules: it is holding on to a person.
More than breathing: length of days, land, children, and above all closeness to God. In v. 20 the Hebrew says literally that he “is your life”; the NRSV gives “that means life to you”.
vv: See, I have set before you today life and prosperity, death and adversity.
“Today” comes four times in this reading. Moses speaks as if the choice were being made at this very moment, and each generation hearing the book read is placed in the same moment.
Choose life so that you and your descendants may live,
God gives the answer to his own question: he tells them what to choose. And the choice reaches beyond the one who makes it, to children not yet born.
loving the Lord your God, obeying him, and holding fast to him;
Here is what choosing life means in practice: three verbs of relationship.
ch: The Catechism says that the way of Christ leads to life and a contrary way leads to destruction, and that the “two ways” have always had a place in the Church's teaching (CCC 1696, citing Deuteronomy 30:15–20). The Didache, one of the oldest Christian writings, opens with the words that there are two ways, one of life and one of death. St John Paul II applies Moses' words directly to our time as a call to be unconditionally for life (Evangelium Vitae 28). God made us able to choose, and this is why our choices matter so much (CCC 1730–1733).

r.h: Take up their cross daily
set: Peter has just said that Jesus is “the Messiah of God” (9:20). Immediately Jesus tells them what this will mean. This is the first of the announcements of his Passion in Luke. The elders, chief priests and scribes are the groups that made up the leading council in Jerusalem, so he is speaking of the action of certain authorities, and no blame falls on the Jewish people (CCC 597).
str: v. 22: the Son of Man must suffer, be rejected, be killed and be raised.
v. 23: the disciple's way: deny, take up, follow.
vv. 24–25: why: two sayings about losing and saving.
kw: A small Greek word which Luke loves. It does not mean blind fate. It speaks of God's saving plan, which runs through the suffering and comes out at the other side.
The verb which Luke will use when Peter denies Jesus (22:57). Either I deny myself, or I end up denying him.
Only Luke has this word in the saying. It changes the picture: the Cross is no longer one heroic moment, but something to take up again each morning.
vv: “If any want to become my followers, let them deny themselves and take up their cross daily and follow me.

He speaks “to them all”: this is not only for apostles or martyrs. For his first hearers a cross was a horror, and no one took one up unless they were going to their death. To deny oneself means no longer putting oneself at the centre.
For those who want to save their life will lose it, and those who lose their life for my sake will save it.
The Greek word for “life” (psychē) also means the self. A life clutched tight is lost, and a life given away is kept. “For my sake” is the key: it is not loss for its own sake.
What does it profit them if they gain the whole world, but lose or forfeit themselves?
A businessman's question. Where Mark says “life”, Luke says “themselves”.
ch: The Catechism teaches that Jesus calls his disciples to “take up their cross and follow him”, for Christ suffered for us leaving an example, and he wants to associate with his sacrifice those who are its first beneficiaries (CCC 618). It also says plainly that taking up one's cross each day and following Jesus is the surest way of penance (CCC 1435). So the daily cross of Lent need not be something unusual. It may be the illness, the difficult relative, the dull duty, accepted with love.

qa: Does Jesus want us to hate ourselves?

No. “Deny themselves” does not mean despising the person God made in his image. It means giving up the claim to be the centre of everything. The saying ends in saving one's life and finding one's true self. The Lord asks for the loss in order to give something greater.
rite: In the Roman calendar 11 February is the commemoration of Our Lady of Lourdes, where Mary appeared to St Bernadette Soubirous in 1858. St John Paul II made this date the World Day of the Sick, first kept in 1993. Today's readings suit the day: the sick who carry their cross daily are often those who teach the rest of us what it means. Today is a good day to visit a sick person or to pray for them.
study: What daily cross are you carrying now? How could you take it up instead of simply putting up with it?
Moses asks you to choose life “today”. Which choice in front of you this week most needs that word?

lead: On the first Friday of Lent, two readings ask what fasting is. In Isaiah the people complain that God has not noticed their fasting, and God replies that it has not touched how they treat their workers. In Matthew Jesus' disciples are asked why they do not fast, and he says that they will, when the bridegroom is taken away. Psalm 51 again gives the heart of it: “a broken and contrite heart, O God, you will not despise.” We fast because we miss the Lord, and we show that we miss him by how we treat the hungry.

r.h: The fast that I choose
set: Chapters 56–66 of Isaiah are thought by many scholars to come from the time after the return from exile, when the people were back in a poor and disappointed land. Fasting days were important to the community then (see Zechariah 7:1–5). The people are devout: they “delight to draw near to God” (v. 2). The prophet's complaint is not about their prayers but about what their prayers leave untouched.
str: vv. 1–2: the prophet is told to shout; the people seem so devout.
v. 3a: the people's complaint: “Why do we fast, but you do not see?”
vv. 3b–5: God's answer: the fasts that do not count.
vv. 6–7: the fast God chooses.
vv. 8–9a: the promise: light, healing, and “Here I am”.
kw: Literally “to afflict the soul”, the standard phrase for fasting, used for the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16:29). It appears in vv. 3 and 5.
“You serve your own interest on your fast day” (v. 3). The word returns twice in the next part of the chapter (v. 13). The fast has been kept for oneself, and God is merely being asked to notice.
What Abraham, Moses and Samuel say when God calls them. Here God says it to the one who calls on him (v. 9). This is the most surprising reward in the chapter.
vv: “Why do we fast, but you do not see? Why humble ourselves, but you do not notice?”
A real complaint, and an honest one. God does not reject the question. He answers it with a look at what is happening at their workplaces on the same day.
Is not this the fast that I choose: to loose the bonds of injustice, to undo the thongs of the yoke, to let the oppressed go free, and to break every yoke?

The prophet does not tell them to stop fasting. He changes what is being fasted from: not only from food, but from the power one holds over others. Jesus reads almost these words at Nazareth (Luke 4:18 adds “to let the oppressed go free” to its quotation of Isaiah 61).
Is it not to share your bread with the hungry, and bring the homeless poor into your house;
The hunger the fast creates makes room for someone else's bread. “Your own kin” at the end of the verse means that those in need are one's own flesh.
Then you shall call, and the Lord will answer; you shall cry for help, and he will say, Here I am.
Their complaint in v. 3 was that God was not looking. Now the promise comes. When the door is opened to the poor, the Lord is found to be standing there.
ch: Jesus' words in Matthew 25 (“I was hungry and you gave me food”) have this chapter behind them. The Catechism lists the works of mercy as the actions that come to the aid of our neighbour in body and soul: feeding the hungry, sheltering the homeless, clothing the naked (CCC 2447), and it recalls that giving alms to the poor is a witness to charity and a work of justice pleasing to God (CCC 2447, 2462). St John Chrysostom told his hearers that the honour of fasting lies in more than abstaining from food: if you see a poor man, take pity on him (in substance).

r.h: When the bridegroom is taken away
set: Just before this, Jesus has called Matthew and eaten with tax collectors and sinners (9:9–13). Now the disciples of John the Baptist come with a question of their own. Pious Jews of the period fasted beyond what the Law required. The Pharisee in Luke's parable fasts twice a week (Luke 18:12). This is a serious question from serious people, and Jesus does not rebuke them.
str: v. 14: the question from John's disciples.
v. 15a: an answer in the form of a question: do guests mourn at a wedding?
v. 15b: the days are coming: then they will fast.
kw: In the prophets the Lord himself is the bridegroom of Israel (Hosea 2:19–20; Isaiah 62:5). Jesus' use of the word for himself is quiet and daring. John the Baptist calls himself the friend of the bridegroom (John 3:29).
Mark and Luke say “fast” here; Matthew says “mourn”. So he draws fasting close to grief, and it recalls “Blessed are those who mourn” (5:4).
A hard word. In the Gospels it comes only in this saying (with its parallels), and it is an early hint in Matthew of a violent end to the wedding.
vv: “Why do we and the Pharisees fast often, but your disciples do not fast?”
Note that they fast “often”, and Jesus does not say that fasting is wrong. His disciples look strange for lacking it.
“The wedding guests cannot mourn as long as the bridegroom is with them, can they?
In a village a wedding was the great feast, and mourning had no place at it. His presence is a time of joy. This is what makes Christian fasting different from a discipline for its own sake.
The days will come when the bridegroom is taken away from them, and then they will fast.
The Church has heard this as her own instruction. We live in those days, between his going and his coming again. Christian fasting has the taste of longing.
ch: The Catechism says that the Lord referred to himself as the “bridegroom” (Mark 2:19), and that the Church is the Bride (CCC 796). The earliest Christians kept fast days: the Didache names Wednesdays and Fridays, and the Friday fast is linked with the Lord's death. The Church's law still makes every Friday and the season of Lent days of penance (Code of Canon Law 1250; CCC 1438). Every Friday, in a small way, the Church remembers the day when the bridegroom was taken away.

study: Whose burden could you lighten this Lent, as your true fast, at home or at work?
If you fast because you miss the bridegroom, how does that change the way you do it?

lead: Today's first reading goes on from where Friday's stopped: the promise to those who feed the hungry. Then Jesus sits down at a banquet with the people nobody wanted. Isaiah says that the one who gives bread will become a watered garden and a repairer of what was broken. Luke shows us a tax collector whose house becomes such a garden. Psalm 86 is the prayer of one who knows that he is “poor and needy”, and this is the one kind of person Jesus says he has come to call.

r.h: The repairer of the breach
set: The chapter that began with fasting moves on to two practical things: how we treat one another (vv. 9b–12), and how we keep God's day (vv. 13–14). For people back from exile, the ruins were not a figure of speech. Jerusalem was still broken (see Nehemiah 1–2), and the keeping of the Sabbath was a chief mark of faithfulness.
str: vv. 9b–10a: if you remove the yoke, the pointing finger and evil speech, and feed the hungry;
vv. 10b–12: then light, guidance, a watered garden and rebuilt ruins.
vv. 13–14a: if you call the Sabbath a delight;
v. 14b: then you shall delight in the Lord.
¶ Both halves have the same “if … then” form. Two promises answer two ways of giving something up.
kw: A breach is a gap in a city wall, where danger comes in. Those who feed the hungry are given a builder's name. Society's broken walls are mended by this kind of work.
“If you call the sabbath a delight.” The same root returns in the promise: “you shall take delight in the Lord.” God's day is not a burden but a joy, and the joy leads to God himself.
The same word as in v. 3. On the fast day, and again on the Sabbath, the trouble is the same: a holy time used for oneself.
vv: if you offer your food to the hungry and satisfy the needs of the afflicted, then your light shall rise in the darkness and your gloom be like the noonday.
The Hebrew says, literally, “if you pour out your soul to the hungry”. It speaks of more than handing over food: one gives oneself.
and you shall be like a watered garden, like a spring of water, whose waters never fail.
People who live in a land with little rain know what this means. The giver does not run dry.
if you call the sabbath a delight and the holy day of the Lord honorable;
Note the order of the chapter: justice first, then worship. They belong together; the chapter refuses to choose between them.
then you shall take delight in the Lord, and I will make you ride upon the heights of the earth;
The language of the Song of Moses, where God “set him atop the heights of the land” (Deuteronomy 32:13). What was promised to Israel long before is offered again to a people who thought it was lost.
ch: The Catechism says that Sunday fulfils the spiritual truth of the Jewish Sabbath (CCC 2175), and that on Sundays the faithful should refrain from work that hinders the joy proper to the Lord's Day and the relaxation of mind and body (CCC 2185). It goes on to say that Sunday is a time for the sick, the elderly and the poor (CCC 2186). So Isaiah's joining of the Sabbath to care for the hungry is still the Church's practice. St John Paul II's letter Dies Domini (1998) is a rich reflection on the joy of Sunday.

r.h: Not the righteous but sinners
set: Levi works at a tax booth. Mark also calls him Levi (Mark 2:14), and Matthew's Gospel tells the same story of a man named Matthew (Matthew 9:9). In Galilee such men collected tolls for the ruler, Herod Antipas. They were widely disliked, for they were seen as working with the powerful and often as taking more than was due. The Pharisees' complaint comes from a real concern for holiness: to share a table was to share life. But the disagreement is about how holiness spreads. They fear that contact with sinners will harm holiness; Jesus shows that holiness can heal.
str: vv. 27–28: the call and the answer.
v. 29: the banquet.
v. 30: the objection.
vv. 31–32: Jesus' answer: the physician and the sick.
kw: Luke's verb in v. 27 suggests more than a passing glance. Jesus looks at the man, and not merely at his job.
Only Luke says that he left everything. A fisherman could go back to his boat, as Peter does later (John 21:3). A tax collector who walked out of his booth had little to go back to.
Only Luke adds “to repentance” at the end of this saying. So the Lord's welcome is not approval of sin, but it comes first, and repentance follows from it.
vv: And he got up, left everything, and followed him.
A man's whole conversion in a single line. There is no speech. The Greek verb for “got up” (anastas) is also a word used for resurrection.
Then Levi gave a great banquet for him in his house;
His first act as a disciple is to throw a party and invite his friends. They may be the only friends he has, and he wants them to meet Jesus. In Luke's Gospel Jesus is often at table.
“Why do you eat and drink with tax collectors and sinners?”
They ask the disciples, not Jesus. The word “their” (“their scribes”) shows that it is a particular group within the Pharisees' circle. Jesus also ate with Pharisees (Luke 7:36; 11:37; 14:1).
“Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick;
He takes a common saying and makes it about himself. No one blames a doctor for visiting the sick. Nor is the point that some people are actually well: the question is who knows that he is sick.
I have come to call not the righteous but sinners to repentance.”
The word “call” is what happened to Levi at his booth, and it is also the word for an invitation to a meal.
ch: The Catechism says that Jesus invites sinners to the table of the Kingdom (CCC 545), and that by receiving sinners at his table he shows in a striking way both God's forgiveness and the return to the heart of the People of God (CCC 1443). It also calls Christ the physician of our souls and bodies (CCC 1421), and says that in the confessional he addresses every sinner personally as the physician tending each of the sick who need him (CCC 1484). St Bede, preaching on Matthew's call, says that Jesus saw him by having mercy and by choosing him (in substance). Pope Francis took the Latin words, miserando atque eligendo, as his motto.

qa: Does this mean that Jesus does not care about sin?

No. Luke says “to repentance”, and Levi left his booth. Jesus does not call the sick “healthy”. But he goes to them, and he does not wait for them to clean themselves up first. The Church asks us to do the same: to hate the sin and go and sit beside the sinner.
study: Who are the people at your parish's door who would not feel welcome at its table? What could you do about it?
Isaiah calls the giver a “repairer of the breach”. What broken wall in your family or neighbourhood could you start to repair this Lent?

lead: The First Sunday of Lent always takes us into the wilderness with Jesus. In this Year B, Mark tells it in two verses, and the other readings explain why it matters. Genesis gives God's covenant after the flood, with the bow in the clouds. Peter says that the water of the flood pointed forward to Baptism. Psalm 25 is the prayer of someone walking a road with God and asking to be taught. Then Mark shows Jesus, fresh from his baptism, driven into the desert among beasts and angels, and coming out to announce the kingdom.

So the theme of this Sunday is water and wilderness: what God saves us through, and where he leads us afterwards. Catechumens who will be baptized at Easter are chosen today in many dioceses, and the rest of us begin to prepare to renew our own promises. The key words are covenant, baptism and repent.

r.h: My bow in the clouds
set: The flood is over, and Noah has left the ark and offered sacrifice (8:20). God has already said in his heart that he will never again destroy every living creature (8:21). Now he says it aloud, as a covenant. This is the first time the Bible describes God establishing a covenant in a full way, and it comes long before Abraham, Moses or Israel. Its partners are Noah, all his descendants and every animal.
Other peoples of the ancient Near East also had flood stories. Many scholars point out how different this one is: the God of Genesis grieves over violence and ends by binding himself to creation.
str: vv. 8–11: the covenant is announced: with whom, and what it promises.
vv. 12–13: the sign: the bow.
vv. 14–15: God will see the bow and remember.
¶ The Lectionary stops at v. 15; vv. 16–17 repeat the promise. In the whole passage, vv. 8–17, the word “covenant” comes seven times.
kw: A binding agreement, and in the Bible a bond between God and his people. This one is striking because God asks nothing in these verses and lays the promise on himself alone.
The same Hebrew word serves for a rainbow and for a war bow. Many interpreters see an image of God hanging up his weapon in the clouds. The text does not say so, but the word allows it.
Not merely to bring to mind, but to act faithfully on what is remembered. It comes in v. 15: “I will remember my covenant.” The sign is for God as well as for us.
vv: “As for me, I am establishing my covenant with you and your descendants after you,
“As for me”: the initiative is all on God's side. Noah says nothing in this whole passage.
and with every living creature that is with you,
The animals are named as covenant partners too: “the birds, the domestic animals, and every animal of the earth”. God's care reaches to all that lives.
I have set my bow in the clouds, and it shall be a sign of the covenant between me and the earth.
The God who sends the rain has also pledged himself in the rain. The sign appears just when the clouds are most threatening.
I will remember my covenant that is between me and you and every living creature of all flesh;
This is the language of Lent: our hope does not rest on our having remembered God but on his remembering us.
ch: The Catechism teaches that the covenant with Noah expresses the principle of God's saving plan towards the nations, and that it remains in force during the times of the nations until the universal proclamation of the Gospel (CCC 56–58). In other words, God has never left any people without care. For Christians this covenant is a first step towards the new and eternal covenant in the blood of Christ, of which we hear at every Mass.

r.h: Teach me your paths
set: Psalm 25 is an acrostic prayer: in Hebrew its verses follow, more or less, the letters of the alphabet. It joins a plea for guidance with a plea for forgiveness. Today's verses make a small school of prayer: first the request to be taught, then the request to be remembered with mercy, then a statement of who God is.
str: vv. 4–5: teach me, lead me.
vv. 6–7: remember your mercy, do not remember my sins.
vv. 8–9: God teaches sinners and the humble.
kw: The psalm's chief word, used of God's “ways” and of the road a person walks. On the First Sunday of Lent it fits the wilderness road.
Three times in vv. 6–7: remember your mercy; do not remember my sins; remember me. The same verb as in the first reading: God remembers his covenant.
People who are poor and know that they depend on God. These are the ones whom God can teach (v. 9).
vv: Make me to know your ways, O Lord; teach me your paths.
This is a prayer for Lent's first week. It asks for no great things, only to be shown the road.
Do not remember the sins of my youth or my transgressions; according to your steadfast love remember me,
A beautiful distinction: forget what I have done, but do not forget me.
Good and upright is the Lord; therefore he instructs sinners in the way.
“Therefore”: the logic is surprising. Because God is good, he does not avoid sinners. He teaches them. The same logic brought Jesus to Levi's table.
ch: The Church sings this psalm on this Sunday as the prayer of those who begin the Lenten journey. Its refrain, from v. 10, joins God's “steadfast love and faithfulness” with those who keep his covenant, and so links directly to Noah. The Catechism says of Christian prayer that it is a covenant relationship between God and man in Christ (CCC 2564). In the same spirit we can make v. 4 a daily prayer for the forty days.

r.h: Saved through water
set: 1 Peter is addressed to Christians scattered through Asia Minor (1:1), who were being slandered and treated as outsiders. The letter comes to us under the name of Peter. Many scholars think that it was written by a disciple in Peter's name, or with the help of a secretary such as Silvanus (5:12); others hold that it comes from Peter himself. It has so much to say about Baptism that some scholars think it draws on baptismal preaching. Here the author encourages his suffering readers by pointing to Christ, who also suffered unjustly and is now in glory.
str: v. 18: Christ's death, once for all, and his being made alive.
vv. 19–20: the proclamation to the spirits in prison; Noah's days.
v. 21: Baptism, prefigured by the ark.
v. 22: Christ at the right hand of God, with all powers subject to him.
kw: Christ's death is not repeated and does not need to be.

The NRSV says “which this prefigured”. The event of the flood is a pattern, and Baptism is what corresponds to it. This is one of the New Testament's clearest examples of reading Old Testament events as signs of Christ's saving work.
A rare word. It may mean an appeal or request to God, as in the NRSV, or a solemn commitment made to him, as in a baptismal promise. Both are true of Baptism.
vv: For Christ also suffered for sins once for all, the righteous for the unrighteous, in order to bring you to God.
A note on the text: some ancient manuscripts read “suffered”, and others “died”. The NRSV has the first and the POC the second. The purpose is the important thing: “to bring you to God”.
in which also he went and made a proclamation to the spirits in prison,
One of the hardest verses in the New Testament. See the question below.
in which a few, that is, eight persons, were saved through water.

The water that destroyed was also the water that carried the ark. The Fathers noticed the “eight”: St Justin connects the eight with the eighth day, the day of the Resurrection, on which Christians gather.
And baptism, which this prefigured, now saves you
A bold statement: Baptism saves. But the author immediately explains that this is not a washing of the skin, and that its power comes “through the resurrection of Jesus Christ”.
who has gone into heaven and is at the right hand of God, with angels, authorities, and powers made subject to him.
For readers who felt powerless, this is the point of it all. Whatever frightens them has already been put under Christ.
ch: The Catechism says that the Church has seen in Noah's ark a prefiguring of salvation by Baptism, and it quotes this passage (CCC 1219). The blessing of baptismal water at the Easter Vigil recalls that the waters of the great flood were made a sign of the waters of Baptism (CCC 1219). The Catechism lists the flood and Noah's ark among the examples of typological reading (CCC 1094). And in teaching on Christ's descent among the dead, it refers to this passage: he went there as Saviour, proclaiming the Good News to the spirits imprisoned there (CCC 632).

r.h: Driven into the wilderness
set: Mark has just told of Jesus' baptism, with the heavens torn open and the voice calling him “my Son, the Beloved” (1:9–11). The next word is “immediately”. Matthew and Luke give the dialogue with the tempter and the three temptations. Mark gives none of this, and does not even mention fasting. He gives only the bare scene, and then, with John in prison, Jesus' first words in this Gospel.
str: vv. 12–13: the wilderness: the Spirit, Satan, the beasts, the angels.
v. 14a: John is arrested.
vv. 14b–15: Jesus comes to Galilee and proclaims the good news.
¶ The two parts belong together. The Jesus who announces the kingdom has already faced its enemy.
kw: The same verb Mark uses when Jesus casts out demons. It is a strong word: the Spirit thrusts Jesus into the place of testing. The POC says “led” (നയിച്ചു), but the Greek is sharper.
Both meanings. God tests in order to prove and strengthen, and Satan tempts in order to bring down. Here the same forty days hold both.
“After John was arrested” is literally “after John was handed over”. Mark uses the same verb for what will be done to Jesus (9:31; 14:41). John's way is a preview of his.
More than being sorry. Turn your whole mind around. Alongside it stands “believe”: pisteuete calls for trust in the good news.
vv: And the Spirit immediately drove him out into the wilderness.
The same Spirit who came down like a dove now pushes him out. Being God's beloved does not exempt one from the desert. It may be what leads there.
He was in the wilderness forty days, tempted by Satan; and he was with the wild beasts; and the angels waited on him.

Forty recalls the rain of Noah's flood (Genesis 7:12), Moses on the mountain (Exodus 34:28), Elijah's walk (1 Kings 19:8) and Israel's years (Deuteronomy 8:2). Only Mark has the beasts. They may show the danger of the place, as Psalm 91:11–13 pictures angels and wild beasts together, or a peace restored as in Eden and in Isaiah 11:6. The text does not decide between these, and the two may stand side by side.
Now after John was arrested, Jesus came to Galilee, proclaiming the good news of God,
The arrest of the prophet does not silence the message. It is at that moment that Jesus begins.
and saying, “The time is fulfilled, and the kingdom of God has come near; repent, and believe in the good news.”

These are his first recorded words in Mark, and they sum up the Gospel. “Time” here is kairos, the moment of decision that Paul spoke of on Ash Wednesday. God's rule is close. Then come two commands, and it is significant that the announcement comes before them: God acts first, and repentance is our answer.
ch: The Catechism teaches that Jesus, the new Adam, remained faithful where the first Adam gave in to temptation, and that he fulfils Israel's vocation, as Israel had tempted God during forty years in the desert (CCC 538–539). “By the solemn forty days of Lent the Church unites herself each year to the mystery of Jesus in the desert” (CCC 540). It quotes Mark 1:15 at the start of Jesus' proclamation of the Kingdom (CCC 541) and as the call to conversion (CCC 1427).

St Augustine says, in a passage read in the Office of Readings on this Sunday, that in Christ we were tempted, and in him we overcome: he took on our temptations so as to give us his victory (in substance).

qa: Who are the “spirits in prison” in 1 Peter 3:19?

There are several readings. St Augustine thought that Christ, in spirit, preached through Noah to the people of Noah's day. Many Fathers and the Catechism connect the verse with Christ's descent among the dead after his death, where he brought the Good News to the just who had gone before (CCC 632–635). Many modern scholars think that “spirits” refers to rebellious powers, connected with Genesis 6 and with Jewish writings such as 1 Enoch, and that the “proclamation” is Christ's announcement of victory. The verse remains difficult, but all agree on its message: there is no place, not even among the dead, where Christ's saving work does not reach.
Wasn't there a rainbow before the flood?

Genesis is not explaining how rainbows work. The rainbow is a natural sight that the story takes up and gives a meaning. In the same way, bread, water and oil existed before the Church took them up into her sacraments. From now on, whenever a person sees the bow after a storm, they are to think of God's promise.
If God leads us into temptation, why do we pray “lead us not into temptation”?

God does not tempt anyone to do evil (James 1:13). In Mark the Spirit leads Jesus into the wilderness, and it is Satan who tempts him there. The Catechism explains the prayer in the Our Father as a plea not to enter into temptation and not to give way to it (CCC 2846–2849). Jesus has gone through this ahead of us, and he prays with us (see Hebrews 4:15).
rite: In the Roman Rite this Sunday has a clear baptismal note. In many dioceses the bishop today celebrates the Rite of Election, in which catechumens are called by name and enrol for Baptism at Easter. Lent's “double character” (Sacrosanctum Concilium 109) is seen today: the Elect prepare to go down into the water, and the rest of us prepare to renew our promises at the Easter Vigil. The Collect asks that we may grow in understanding of the riches hidden in Christ. The Alleluia and Gloria are not sung. The memorial of Sts Cyril and Methodius, which falls on this day, is not kept this year because it is Sunday; their translation of the Scriptures for the Slavs is a good reminder of what the word of God does for a people. Pray today for the catechumens of your diocese by name if you can, and if you do not know your own date of Baptism, find it out this week.
study: God bound himself to “every living creature”. What does this ask of you in your care of creation?
What is your wilderness at this time? Who are the “wild beasts”, and who are the “angels”?
Jesus begins with “repent, and believe”. Which of the two do you find harder this Lent, and why?
Do you know the date of your Baptism? How could you and your family prepare to renew your promises at Easter?

lead: The first full weekday of Lent after the First Sunday puts one plain question before us: what does holiness look like on an ordinary day? Leviticus answers with wages, courts, the deaf and the blind, and a grudge kept in the heart. Matthew answers with the hungry, the stranger and the prisoner, and with the astonishing word of the King: “you did it to me.” God’s holiness is not kept away from daily life. It is met there. The key words are holy, neighbor and the least.

r.h: Be holy, for I am holy
set: Leviticus 17–26 is often called the Holiness Code, because of its refrain that Israel must be holy as God is holy. Chapter 19 is its heart. It mixes worship and ethics without any sense of changing the subject: the sabbath stands next to fair weights, and the offerings next to care for the poor.

The Lectionary takes the opening call, then the block of commands about the neighbor. Much of the chapter echoes the Ten Commandments, here applied to the life of a village: its workers, its courts, its gossip.
str: vv. 1–2: the call to the whole congregation: “You shall be holy.”
vv. 11–12: honesty, in dealings and in oaths.
vv. 13–14: the worker, the deaf and the blind.
vv. 15–16: the court and the tongue.
vv. 17–18: the heart, ending in the command to love.
¶ Each of these four small groups closes with the same words, “I am the Lord”. Every duty to a neighbor is signed with God’s own name.
kw: The basic idea is set apart, belonging to God. Israel is holy not by being better than others but by being his. Then that belonging has to show in how people live.

The fellow member of the community, the person next to you. Later in this chapter the same love is commanded for the resident alien (19:34). Jesus opens the word wider still in the parable of the Samaritan (Luke 10:29–37).
Not a command to love oneself first, but a measure: the care I naturally take for my own life is the measure of what I owe my neighbor.
vv: You shall be holy, for I the Lord your God am holy.
This is the root of the chapter. Moral life begins not from a list but from who God is. 1 Peter 1:16 passes the same call on to Christians.
and you shall not keep for yourself the wages of a laborer until morning.

A day laborer lived on that day’s pay. Holding it back overnight meant a hungry family. The Catechism names the withholding of a just wage as a possible grave injustice and cites this verse (CCC 2434).
You shall not revile the deaf or put a stumbling block before the blind; you shall fear your God
The deaf cannot hear the curse and the blind cannot see who laid the block. The sin can go undetected by its victim, but not by God.
You shall not hate in your heart anyone of your kin; you shall reprove your neighbor, or you will incur guilt yourself.
The law reaches inside. Silent hatred is the sin, and honest correction is one of its cures (compare Matthew 18:15).
but you shall love your neighbor as yourself: I am the Lord.

Rabbi Akiba called this a great principle of the Torah (in substance). Jesus joined it to the love of God as the second great commandment (Matthew 22:39), and Paul says the commandments are summed up in it (Romans 13:9).
ch: The Catechism teaches that the whole Law hangs on the two commandments of love (CCC 2055). The Second Vatican Council took up “Be holy” for every baptized person, not for a few: all the faithful are called to the fullness of the Christian life (Lumen Gentium 40; CCC 2013). This is a useful text for an examination of conscience in Lent, since it goes through work, speech and the secret heart.

r.h: You did it to me
set: This is the last teaching of Jesus in Matthew before the Passion. It closes the discourse on the end of the age (chapters 24–25), and only Matthew has it. The scene joins two images from the Old Testament: the Son of Man who receives everlasting dominion over all peoples (Daniel 7:13–14), and God as the shepherd who judges within his flock, “between sheep and sheep” (Ezekiel 34:17).
str: vv. 31–33: the King on his throne; all the nations; the separation.
vv. 34–40: “Come”: six works of love, the surprise of the righteous, and the King’s answer.
vv. 41–45: “depart”: the same list, the same surprise, the opposite answer.
v. 46: two destinies.
kw: Often this word means the Gentiles, but here the judgment reaches everyone. Scholars discuss the exact scope. The sense of the scene is that no one stands outside it.
The superlative of “small”. These are people with no standing, who have nothing to give back.

Some commentators, ancient and modern, take these to be Christ’s disciples, above all those sent out in poverty (compare 10:40–42). Others take them to be all who are in need. The Church’s teaching applies the text to every person in need, without exception (Gaudium et Spes 27).
vv: Come, you that are blessed by my Father, inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world;

The kingdom is an inheritance, prepared long before anyone earned anything. The works that follow do not buy it. Done in grace, they are how the gift is received and kept, and their merit is itself God's gift (CCC 2009).
Lord, when was it that we saw you hungry and gave you food,
The righteous are surprised. They did not serve the poor as a clever way of serving Christ. They simply saw a hungry person and gave food.
Truly I tell you, just as you did it to one of the least of these who are members of my family, you did it to me.
Jesus does not say “it is as if”. He says “to me”. This is the centre of the passage.
You that are accursed, depart from me into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels;

Compare v. 34. The kingdom was prepared for human beings. The fire was prepared for the devil and his angels. God predestines no one to hell (CCC 1037). Notice too what these people are condemned for: not for cruelty, but for doing nothing.
ch: The Catechism draws from this passage the works of mercy (CCC 2447) and the warning that we are separated from God if we fail to meet the serious needs of the poor and the little ones (CCC 1033). It also quotes St John of the Cross: at the evening of life we shall be judged on love (CCC 1022). St John Chrysostom told his people that the Christ they honor on the altar is the same Christ they neglect when he is cold and naked at the door (in substance), and the Catechism links the Eucharist with the poor in the same spirit (CCC 1397). Sulpicius Severus tells how St Martin of Tours, still a catechumen, shared his cloak with a beggar and that night saw Christ wearing it.

qa: Does this mean we are saved by good works?

No. The kingdom is “prepared” and “inherited”, and salvation is the gift of God’s grace (Ephesians 2:8). But a faith that never feeds anyone is not the faith the New Testament means. Paul’s own phrase is “faith working through love” (Galatians 5:6). Grace comes first, and it bears fruit; and by that same grace our good works truly merit eternal life, as his gift and not as our own achievement (CCC 2008–2010).
study: Leviticus 19 goes through wages, courts, gossip and grudges. Which of these touches my own life this Lent?
Who are “the least” within my reach today, the ones who cannot repay me? What one work of mercy can I do for them this week?

lead: Both readings are about words. In Isaiah, God’s word goes out like rain and does not come back empty. In Matthew, Jesus warns against the piling up of words and gives us a few that are enough. God’s word comes down to us, does its work, and returns; the Our Father is the word that carries us back to him. The key words are word, Father and forgive.

r.h: My word shall not return to me empty
set: Isaiah 40–55, the Book of Consolation, speaks to the Jews in exile in Babylon in the sixth century BC. Many scholars think it comes from an unnamed prophet of the exile, in the tradition of Isaiah. Chapter 55 is its closing invitation, opening with “Ho, everyone who thirsts, come to the waters” (55:1).

The exiles had reason to doubt. Jerusalem lay in ruins, and God’s promises looked like words that had come to nothing. Just before our reading God says that his ways and thoughts are as high above ours as the heavens are above the earth (55:9). These two verses then show that what is high does not stay high: it comes down.
str: v. 10: the picture: rain and snow come down, water the earth, and give seed and bread.
v. 11: the comparison: so shall my word be.
¶ It is one long sentence in Hebrew, built on “as” and “so”.
kw: In Hebrew this means both a word and a thing done. God’s word is not a sound that fades. It acts: “God said” and it was so (Genesis 1).
Empty-handed, with nothing to show. It is the word for someone who comes back from a journey having gained nothing.
To bring something to a good end. The word itself, sent out on an errand like a messenger, finishes the task it was given.
vv: For as the rain and the snow come down from heaven, and do not return there until they have watered the earth,
The prophet is careful with the order: the rain goes back up only after the ground has drunk. Growth is slow and hidden, and the farmer does not see it happen.
giving seed to the sower and bread to the eater,
The gift is double: bread for today, seed for next year.
so shall my word be that goes out from my mouth; it shall not return to me empty, but it shall accomplish that which I purpose,
The promise does not say that we will always see the result, or see it soon. It says that the word will do what God intends.
ch: Christians hear in this picture the whole path of Jesus, the Word made flesh. He says, “I came from the Father and have come into the world; again, I am leaving the world and am going to the Father” (John 16:28). The Second Vatican Council speaks of the great force and power in the word of God, the support and energy of the Church (Dei Verbum 21; CCC 131). For those who preach and teach, and for parents who repeat the faith to children who seem not to listen, this is a verse of real comfort.

r.h: Pray then in this way
set: We are in the Sermon on the Mount. Jesus has just spoken about three practices of Jewish piety: almsgiving, prayer and fasting (6:1–18), the same three the Church takes up in Lent. In each he says: do it for the Father, who sees in secret. At the centre of that teaching he sets the Our Father.

Luke has a shorter form of the prayer (Luke 11:2–4), and Matthew’s longer form is the one the Church prays. Matthew’s setting is a teaching on how to pray; Luke’s is the disciples’ request, “Lord, teach us to pray”.
str: vv. 7–8: not many words: the Father already knows.
vv. 9–10: three petitions for God: his name, his kingdom, his will.
vv. 11–13: our needs: bread, forgiveness, protection.
vv. 14–15: a comment on one petition alone: forgiveness.
kw: The word is rare and its exact meaning is uncertain; it may imitate the sound of babbling. The warning is against the idea that a great many words can wear God down.

Found almost nowhere outside this prayer, so its sense is debated: for today, for tomorrow, or what we need to live. The Catechism gathers the meanings: our needs for this day, and also, taken literally as “super-essential”, the Bread of Life, the Body of Christ (CCC 2837).
Matthew’s word is “debts”, Luke’s is “sins”. In the Aramaic of that time the word for a debt was also used for sin. We stand before God as people who owe what they cannot pay.
vv: for your Father knows what you need before you ask him.
Then why ask? Not to inform God, but because prayer changes the one who prays: it makes us children who trust.
Pray then in this way: Our Father in heaven, hallowed be your name.
“Our”, not “my”: no one prays this prayer alone. “Hallowed be” asks God himself to make his name known as holy (compare Ezekiel 36:23; CCC 2807–2808).
And forgive us our debts, as we also have forgiven our debtors.

This is the one petition with a condition in it, and the only one Jesus goes back to explain (vv. 14–15). The Catechism says that God’s mercy cannot penetrate a heart that refuses to forgive (CCC 2840).
And do not bring us to the time of trial, but rescue us from the evil one.

A note on the text. The closing words “For the kingdom and the power and the glory are yours” are not in the oldest manuscripts of Matthew and are not printed in the NRSV’s main text or in the POC. A form of them appears in the very old Didache, and the Roman Mass says similar words after the prayer that follows the Our Father. “The evil one” is a person, Satan, not an abstraction (CCC 2851).
ch: Tertullian called the Lord’s Prayer “truly the summary of the whole gospel”, and St Thomas Aquinas called it the most perfect of prayers (CCC 2761, 2763). The closing section of the Catechism is a commentary on it, petition by petition (CCC 2759–2865). The Church prays it at every Mass as the family’s preparation for Communion.

qa: If Jesus warned against many words, why do Catholics say the Rosary or a litany?

The warning is against the belief that the amount of words will force God’s hand. Jesus himself in Gethsemane “prayed for the third time, saying the same words” (Matthew 26:44). The Catechism says that the repeated invocation of a holy name is not heaping up empty phrases, but a holding fast to the word (CCC 2668). Repetition said with love is like a child who says the same thing to a mother many times.
study: Where have I seen God’s word working slowly, long after it was first spoken to me?
Which line of the Our Father is hardest for me to say honestly today? Whom do I need to forgive so that I can say it?

lead: This is the Lenten reading par excellence: a whole foreign city turns to God at the preaching of a reluctant prophet. Jesus takes up that story and turns it toward his hearers: those people listened to Jonah, and someone greater than Jonah is here. The question for Lent is simple. Nineveh needed five Hebrew words; how many have I heard? The key words are turn, sign and greater.

r.h: Who knows? God may relent
set: The Book of Jonah is short and unlike the other prophets: it is a story about a prophet, not a collection of his sayings. A prophet named Jonah son of Amittai appears in 2 Kings 14:25, in the eighth century BC. Many Catholic scholars read the book as a teaching story, written later, after the exile. Its message stands in either case.

Nineveh was a capital of Assyria, the empire that destroyed the northern kingdom of Israel, and it stood in Israel’s memory as a city of cruelty; the prophet Nahum sings of its fall (612 BC). Jonah has already fled from this mission once, and has been swallowed and brought back (chapters 1–2). Now comes the second call. Chapter 4 will show why he ran: he did not want these people forgiven.
str: vv. 1–3a: the second call, and this time Jonah goes.
vv. 3b–4: the great city and the very short sermon.
v. 5: the people believe and fast, from the greatest to the least.
vv. 6–9: the king and his decree.
v. 10: God sees, and does not do what he had said.
kw: The Old Testament’s great word for conversion. It is about direction: you were walking one way, and you turn around. Here it is used of the people (v. 8) and of God (v. 9).
From a verb meaning to overturn, used of Sodom (Genesis 19:25). But it can also mean to be changed, and many have noticed the double sense: Nineveh was indeed overturned in forty days, by conversion.

Said of God, this describes in human language his turning from a threat when people turn from their sin. Jeremiah states the rule: “if that nation, concerning which I have spoken, turns from its evil, I will change my mind” (18:8).
vv: The word of the Lord came to Jonah a second time,
The God who gives a second chance to Nineveh has first given one to his own prophet.
Forty days more, and Nineveh shall be overthrown!
In Hebrew the sermon is five words long. There is no call to repent and no offer of mercy in it. A note on the text. The Hebrew says forty days, while the Greek Old Testament says three.
And the people of Nineveh believed God;
They respond before the king does, and before anyone tells them what to do. Foreigners do at once what Israel’s prophet had run away from.
Who knows? God may relent and change his mind;

The king claims nothing. Repentance does not put God under an obligation; it hopes in his mercy. Joel uses the same words (Joel 2:14). Even the animals in sackcloth (v. 8), with their touch of humor, show how complete the turning was.
When God saw what they did, how they turned from their evil ways,
God looks at what they did: not at the sackcloth, but at the turning from evil and violence (v. 8).
ch: The Catechism teaches that Jesus’ call to conversion does not aim first at outward works, “sackcloth and ashes”, fasting and mortification, but at conversion of the heart; without this such works remain sterile, and true interior conversion in turn seeks expression in visible signs (CCC 1430). Lent is one of the Church’s seasons of penance (CCC 1438). The Syriac Churches, including our Syro-Malabar and Malankara brothers and sisters in Kerala, keep a special three-day fast in memory of the repentance of Nineveh, before Lent begins.

r.h: Something greater than Jonah is here
set: Luke’s setting explains the saying. Jesus has driven out a demon, some have said he does it by Beelzebul, and “others, to test him, kept demanding from him a sign from heaven” (11:16). Now, with the crowds growing, he answers. He has already given signs. The trouble is what the demand for one more sign hides.
“This generation” in the Gospels means those who refuse to hear, in that place and time. It is a warning to every listener in every age, not a verdict on a people (CCC 597–598).
str: v. 29: no sign but the sign of Jonah.
v. 30: Jonah was a sign to Nineveh; so the Son of Man will be.
v. 31: the queen of the South.
v. 32: the people of Nineveh.
kw: A mark that points beyond itself. A sign demanded as proof is different from a sign received in faith.
The queen of Sheba (1 Kings 10:1–13), who came from far away to test Solomon with hard questions. A foreign woman and a foreign city are the witnesses in this court.
The Greek is neuter: not “someone” but “something greater”. It points to what is happening among them in Jesus, greater than wisdom and greater than prophecy.
vv: For just as Jonah became a sign to the people of Nineveh, so the Son of Man will be to this generation.

In Luke the sign is Jonah himself and his preaching; Luke says nothing here about the sea monster. Matthew draws out the three days and three nights (Matthew 12:40). The two fit together: the one who preaches is the one who will go down into death and rise.
The people of Nineveh will rise up at the judgment with this generation and condemn it,
The picture is of a court. The foreigners stand as witnesses for the prosecution, not because they were holy, but because they repented.
because they repented at the proclamation of Jonah, and see, something greater than Jonah is here!
The argument goes from the lesser to the greater. Nineveh had a reluctant prophet and no miracles. We have the Son of Man.
ch: The Catechism says that only the divine identity of Jesus’ person can justify a claim like “something greater than Jonah” and “greater than Solomon” (CCC 590). It also notes that Jesus speaks of the sign of Jonah when he announces his Resurrection on the third day (CCC 994). So the sign that the Lord gives his Church is the Paschal mystery itself, toward which all of Lent is walking.

qa: Does God change his mind?

Scripture says both things. “God is not a human being, that he should lie, or a mortal, that he should change his mind” (Numbers 23:19), and also that God “changed his mind” about Nineveh (3:10). God’s will to save does not change. The threat was given so that it would never have to be carried out. When we change, we meet that same will as mercy instead of as judgment. Scripture’s human language tells us that God truly responds to his people.
study: Jonah ran from a mission because he did not want certain people forgiven. Is there anyone I secretly do not want God to forgive?
What “sign” am I waiting for before I turn to God in earnest? What has he already given me?

lead: A queen with no one to turn to and a Teacher who says “Ask” stand side by side today. Esther prays alone, with her life in danger and nothing to rely on but God. Jesus tells us why such a prayer is not foolish: we are speaking to a Father. Both readings teach the boldness of those who know their poverty and know whom they are asking. The key words are alone, ask and how much more.

r.h: No helper but you
set: The Book of Esther comes to us in two forms. The Hebrew tells of a Jewish queen in the Persian court who saves her people from a decree of destruction planned by the king’s minister Haman; it never names God. The Greek form adds six longer passages, including the prayers of Mordecai and Esther, so that what happens is seen to be God’s work. The Catholic Church receives the book with these additions as Scripture.

The numbering is confusing. Lectionaries call this passage C:12–25. The NRSV, following the older numbering from St Jerome’s Latin Bible, prints it as chapter 14. The wording also differs a little from one Bible to another, because the Greek and Latin texts differ.

The situation: the decree has gone out. Mordecai has asked Esther to go to the king, and no one may enter his presence uninvited on pain of death. Esther asks all the Jews of Susa to fast for three days with her. Then, before going in, she prays.
str: C:12 (14:1): Esther, in mortal fear, flees to the Lord.
C:14–16 (14:3–5): “no helper but you”, and the memory of what God has done for Israel.
C:23–25 (14:12–14): “Remember”: a request for courage and for words, and a cry to be saved.
kw: In the Greek, Esther is “the one who is alone”. She is a queen in a palace with servants around her, yet at this hour she is utterly alone.
The word the Greek Psalms often use of God. “No helper but you” is not despair. It is the most exact prayer she can say.
Her name for the king, who holds the power of life and death over her. She does not pretend that he is not dangerous.
vv: O my Lord, you only are our king; help me, who am alone and have no helper but you,
She is the wife of the most powerful king of her world, and she says there is only one King. That sentence will give her the courage to walk into the throne room.
for my danger is in my hand.
This is an idiom: her life is on the line, in her own hands.
Remember, O Lord; make yourself known in this time of our affliction, and give me courage,
She does not ask to be spared the task. She asks for courage to do it. This is a good model of prayer in fear.
Put eloquent speech in my mouth before the lion,
Prayer and practical action are not opposites. She has fasted and prayed, and she will still dress, walk in, and speak carefully (Esther 5).
But save us by your hand, and help me, who am alone and have no helper but you, O Lord.
She moves from “me” to “us” and back: her own fear and her people’s danger are one prayer.
ch: The Catechism teaches that humility is the foundation of prayer (CCC 2559), and Esther prays from that place. She is a model of intercession: one person who stands before power for the sake of many. Christian writers and artists, above all in the Middle Ages, often saw in Esther a figure of Mary, the queen who intercedes for her people. Today’s reading also reminds us of Israel’s long experience of threatened destruction. We read it with reverence for the Jewish people, who still remember Esther each year at the feast of Purim.

r.h: How much more will your Father give
set: We are near the end of the Sermon on the Mount. The sermon has asked a great deal: love of enemies, purity of heart, trust instead of worry. Here Jesus gives the means to live it: ask. Then he sums up the whole with one rule of life. The words “this is the law and the prophets” (v. 12) reach back to the start of his teaching: “I have come not to abolish but to fulfill” (5:17).
str: v. 7: three commands: ask, search, knock.
v. 8: three promises, for “everyone”.
vv. 9–10: two questions about a father and a child.
v. 11: the argument: how much more.
v. 12: the Golden Rule.
kw: All three are present imperatives in Greek, which suggest something continuing: keep asking, keep searching, keep knocking. Each is a stronger action than the last.
Said to the disciples in passing, and it is said without any drama. Even sinful parents know how to give good things to their children. The argument depends on it.
Luke’s parallel reads: “how much more will the heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit” (Luke 11:13). Good things in the end means God’s own gift of himself.
vv: Ask, and it will be given you; search, and you will find; knock, and the door will be opened for you.
“It will be given” and “it will be opened” do not say who does it, but the passive points to God, as often in the Gospels.
Is there anyone among you who, if your child asks for bread, will give a stone?
Jesus asks his hearers to look at what they know from home. Bread and fish were everyday food by the lake. A father who gave a stone or a snake would not be a father.
how much more will your Father in heaven give good things to those who ask him!
This argument from the lesser to the greater is the centre of the passage. The best parent we have known is only the beginning of what God is.
In everything do to others as you would have them do to you; for this is the law and the prophets.

Earlier Jewish teaching already said this in negative form: “what you hate, do not do to anyone” (Tobit 4:15), and Rabbi Hillel said much the same (in substance). Jesus states it as a positive duty: do not wait, begin.
ch: The Catechism says that Jesus teaches filial boldness in prayer (CCC 2610), and that the Gospel’s moral law is summed up in the Golden Rule (CCC 1970; compare 1789). St Augustine wrote to the widow Proba that God wants our desire to be exercised in prayer, so that we may grow large enough to receive what he is preparing to give (in substance; Letter 130). Those words give an answer to anyone who feels that prayer takes too long.

qa: I asked and knocked, and nothing happened. Was the promise false?

This is an honest question, and the Catechism takes it up: we often ask wrongly, or for what is not good for us, or we want the gift more than the Giver (CCC 2735–2737). Jesus himself asked for the cup to pass, and he received not an escape but the Resurrection. The promise is that the Father always gives good things, not that he always gives the thing I named. Asking again, even in the dark, is itself part of what he is giving.
study: Esther says that she has “no helper but you”. Is that my true prayer, or do I keep God as a last resort behind other plans?
Is there something I stopped asking God for because I grew tired? What would it mean to keep knocking?

lead: On this Friday of Lent the readings look at where the heart is now. Ezekiel tells a discouraged people that no one is trapped by the past, neither the sinner by his sins nor the good man by his good record. Jesus takes the commandment against murder down to its root in anger, and then sends us away from the altar to make peace. The key words are turn, live and be reconciled.

r.h: Have I any pleasure in the death of the wicked?
set: Ezekiel was a priest taken to Babylon with the first deportation of 597 BC (1:1–3). Jerusalem was then destroyed in 587. Among the exiles a bitter saying went round: “The parents have eaten sour grapes, and the children’s teeth are set on edge” (18:2). It meant: we are paying for our ancestors’ sins, and nothing we do can matter.

Chapter 18 answers that saying. Each person stands before God on his own account, and the present turning of a life counts. Scripture also knows of the way sin harms later generations, and Ezekiel does not deny that. He is speaking to a despair that was using it as an excuse. The words “live” and “die” here mean life and death under God’s covenant, in a time when belief in life after death had not yet become clear.
str: vv. 21–22: the wicked who turn shall live.
v. 23: the central question from God.
v. 24: the righteous who turn away.
vv. 25–28: “The way of the Lord is unfair”: God’s answer, and the same two cases once more.
kw: As so often in the prophets, this is the word for conversion. It runs right through the chapter and appears in both directions: away from sin, and away from righteousness.
The word is used of what someone really delights in. God’s own question denies that he delights in the sinner’s death. Ezekiel 33:11 repeats it on God’s oath.
From a verb meaning to weigh or to measure. The people say God’s scales are not true. God turns the charge back to them (v. 25).
vv: None of the transgressions that they have committed shall be remembered against them;
The past really is past. This is the Old Testament’s strong word for what the Church offers in the sacrament of Penance.
Have I any pleasure in the death of the wicked, says the Lord God, and not rather that they should turn from their ways and live?
This is the heart of the reading, and it comes as a question because God wants us to answer it. God “desires everyone to be saved” (1 Timothy 2:4).
Yet you say, “The way of the Lord is unfair.”
It is a very human complaint. It may be heard from the elder brother in the parable of the prodigal son. God’s mercy can look unfair to those who keep accounts.
Because they considered and turned away from all the transgressions that they had committed, they shall surely live; they shall not die.
The verb “considered” is worth noticing. Conversion begins when a person stops, looks honestly at his life, and sees it.
ch: The Church hears in this passage both her hope and her warning. Mortal sin, if not redeemed by repentance and God’s forgiveness, leads to exclusion from Christ’s kingdom; but we must entrust judgment of persons to God’s mercy (CCC 1861). God wills no one to perish, and desires all to come to repentance (CCC 1037; 2 Peter 3:9). Lent is the Church’s time for this “consider and turn”, and the sacrament of Penance is its proper place (CCC 1422–1424).

r.h: First be reconciled
set: Jesus has just said that he came to fulfill the law, not to abolish it (5:17–19). Verse 20 is the heading for what follows, and vv. 21–48 give six examples, each with “You have heard… But I say to you”. Today’s is the first, on murder.

Jesus’ word about the scribes and Pharisees is not an attack on the Jewish people or on the Law. The Pharisees’ own concern for keeping the Law in spirit as well as letter was close to his own (CCC 579). Many scholars think that Matthew writes in a time of tension between his community and other Jewish teachers, and a reader should keep that in mind. Jesus asks his disciples for a righteousness that goes to the root.
str: v. 20: the heading: a greater righteousness.
vv. 21–22: from murder to anger and insult.
vv. 23–24: first example: at the altar.
vv. 25–26: second example: on the way to court.
kw: In Matthew, doing God’s will as a response to his grace: right relations with God and with others. It is a key word of the Sermon on the Mount.
From the Valley of Hinnom beside Jerusalem, once a place of child sacrifice (Jeremiah 7:31). In later Jewish writing and in the Gospels the name is used for final punishment.
The only use of this verb in the New Testament. It is a command, and notice whose duty it is: the one who remembers that the other has something against him.
vv: But I say to you that if you are angry with a brother or sister, you will be liable to judgment;

A note on the text. Many later manuscripts add “without cause”; the oldest do not have it, and neither does the NRSV. The rising list (anger, an insult, “You fool”) is not a table of penalties. It is a way of saying that murder begins here. The word the NRSV renders “insult” is the Aramaic raka, “empty-head”.
So when you are offering your gift at the altar, if you remember that your brother or sister has something against you,
Note that it is not “if you have something against him”. Even if the fault is the other’s, the first step falls to me.
leave your gift there before the altar and go; first be reconciled to your brother or sister, and then come and offer your gift.
For a Galilean the altar was days away in Jerusalem, and that is part of the force of the picture. Jesus is not setting worship aside. “Then come”: he wants the gift, from a reconciled heart.
Come to terms quickly with your accuser while you are on the way to court with him,
There is an urgency. There is still time on the road. A quarrel left alone grows, and so does its cost.
ch: The Catechism teaches that the Lord adds to “You shall not kill” the proscription of anger, hatred and vengeance (CCC 2262), and that from the Sermon on the Mount onward he insists on conversion of heart, reconciliation with one’s brother before presenting an offering on the altar (CCC 2608). The very old Didache tells Christians at odds with one another not to join the Sunday Eucharist until they are reconciled, so that the sacrifice may not be defiled (in substance; ch. 14). At Mass the Sign of Peace keeps this teaching before us.

qa: Does one sin wipe out a whole good life, as Ezekiel seems to say?

Ezekiel is describing a change in the direction of a life, “turning away” and doing the abominable things of the wicked, not a slip. The Church distinguishes mortal and venial sin (CCC 1854–1855). Even a grave sin is not the end, since the same chapter that warns the righteous also promises life to anyone who turns back. What the prophet refuses is the idea that a good record is a bank account against which one may sin.
study: Do I think of myself as trapped by my past, or as safe because of my good record? What does Ezekiel say to me?
Who has something against me? What one step could I take before my next Communion?
