lead: The first week of Lent ends with a covenant and a family likeness. In Deuteronomy God and Israel bind themselves to each other “today”, and Israel becomes his treasured people. In Matthew Jesus shows what the children of such a Father look like: they love even their enemies, because that is what he does. The key words are today, treasured and perfect.

r.h: A people holy to the Lord your God
set: Deuteronomy is presented as Moses’ last address to Israel on the plains of Moab, before they cross into the land. Chapters 12–26 give the long code of laws. Today’s four verses are its closing lines. After all the statutes, Moses reminds the people what they mean: a relationship between God and his people.
str: v. 16: the command: observe with all your heart and soul.
v. 17: what Israel has declared about God.
vv. 18–19: what God has declared about Israel.
¶ It is laid out like a treaty, with each side making a solemn statement of what it will be for the other.
kw: A favourite word of Deuteronomy, and it comes three times here. Every generation that hears these words stands at the covenant “today”. Psalm 95 and Hebrews 3–4 take it up in the same way.

A rare verb form, found in this sense only here (vv. 17–18), and its exact sense is debated. The NRSV’s “obtained the agreement” and the POC’s “declared” (പ്രഖ്യാപിച്ചിരിക്കുന്നു) are both attempts to render a solemn exchange of promises.
A personal treasure, such as a king’s private wealth (1 Chronicles 29:3). It is used for Israel in Exodus 19:5, Deuteronomy 7:6 and Malachi 3:17.
vv: so observe them diligently with all your heart and with all your soul.
These are the words of the great commandment (Deuteronomy 6:5). The laws are to be kept not as an outward task but with one’s whole self.
Today the Lord has obtained your agreement: to be his treasured people, as he promised you, and to keep his commandments;
Being treasured comes first, and it comes as a promise. The commandments are how the treasured live.
and for you to be a people holy to the Lord your God, as he promised.

Holiness here is a promise and not only a demand: “as he promised”. And the honor Israel receives among the nations (v. 19) belongs with this holiness: it is a people set high because it belongs to God.
ch: The Catechism says that the commandments express the implications of belonging to God through the covenant, and that moral existence is a response to the Lord’s loving initiative (CCC 2062). The Second Vatican Council, speaking of the People of God, begins from God’s choice of Israel, and applies to the Church the words of 1 Peter 2:9, “a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, God’s own people” (Lumen Gentium 9; CCC 781–782). The covenant with Israel is not thereby revoked (CCC 121, 839).

r.h: Children of your Father in heaven
set: This is the last of the six “You have heard… But I say to you” sayings, and the peak of them all. Love of neighbor is commanded in Leviticus 19:18. The words “hate your enemy” are not found in the Law. Jesus seems to be quoting a popular reading of the command, which took “neighbor” to imply its opposite. Many scholars also point to a text from Qumran that speaks of hating the sons of darkness.
Jewish Scripture itself had already pointed in Jesus’ direction: help your enemy’s stray animal (Exodus 23:4–5), and feed your enemy when he is hungry (Proverbs 25:21–22, quoted in Romans 12:20).
str: v. 43: the saying they have heard.
v. 44: the command: love and pray.
v. 45: the reason: the Father’s sun and rain.
vv. 46–47: two questions: what more are you doing?
v. 48: the summary.
kw: Not a feeling of liking, which cannot be ordered. It is a will for the other’s good, shown in action. Jesus does not ask us to feel warmly about those who harm us.
This is not only personal rivals. In the setting of v. 44, it includes those who persecute the disciples.
Not flawless, but whole, complete, undivided. Behind it may stand the Hebrew tāmîm, used in Deuteronomy 18:13. Luke’s parallel has “merciful” (Luke 6:36), and that tells us which perfection is meant.
vv: But I say to you, Love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you,

Prayer is where this love begins, and where it may have to stay for a long time. Christians suffer for their faith in many lands. The Lord’s command is to pray for them and for those who wrong them. We can pray for someone whom we cannot yet feel any warmth toward.
so that you may be children of your Father in heaven; for he makes his sun rise on the evil and on the good,
The reason is a family likeness. Children of this Father look like him. The sun is the great daily sermon on the mercy of God.
For if you love those who love you, what reward do you have? Do not even the tax collectors do the same?
Jesus uses the people his hearers looked down on, and he himself ate with them (Matthew 9:10–13). The question is simple: what is different about you?
Be perfect, therefore, as your heavenly Father is perfect.
Compare “You shall be holy, for I the Lord your God am holy” (Leviticus 19:2). The command is impossible by human strength, and that is why the Sermon also teaches us to ask.
ch: The Catechism says that Christ died for us while we were still enemies (Romans 5:10), and that the Lord asks us to love as he does, even our enemies (CCC 1825). The “as” of Matthew 5:48 cannot mean imitating God from outside, but only sharing, in the depths of the heart, in the holiness and mercy of God (CCC 2842). The Council teaches that this perfection is for all the baptized (Lumen Gentium 40; CCC 2013). The first martyr followed his Lord’s example: “Lord, do not hold this sin against them” (Acts 7:60).

qa: Can anyone really be perfect? Is Jesus setting us up to fail?

He is setting a direction and a likeness, not a score to reach by ourselves. Perfection in Matthew means the wholeness of a love with no one left out. It grows through grace all through a life, and we always need the petition “forgive us our debts”. The saints did not think they had arrived, and that is part of why we call them saints.
study: Moses tells Israel that it is God’s “treasured people”. How would my obedience change if I began from that?
Name one person who is hard for me to love. Can I pray for that person by name every day for the rest of Lent?

lead: Every Second Sunday of Lent the Church goes up the mountain of the Transfiguration, after the desert of the First Sunday. This year, in the Year B readings, a second mountain stands beside it: Moriah. The two mountains belong together. On Moriah, Abraham is told to offer “your only son… whom you love”, and God stops his hand. On the high mountain, the Father’s voice says, “This is my Son, the Beloved”, and that Son will not be spared.

St Paul, in between, makes the link explicit: “He who did not withhold his own Son”. The readings are not a pause from the Cross but a glimpse of what lies beyond it. Abraham goes up not knowing, the three disciples go up and come down not understanding, and we are asked with them to “listen to him” on the way to Jerusalem. The key words are beloved, not withheld and listen.

r.h: Your son, your only son, whom you love
set: This is the summit of the story of Abraham. God called him with a promise of descendants (Genesis 12:2), and after long years of waiting Isaac was born. All God’s promises now rest on this one boy. “After these things” God asks for him.

Jewish tradition calls this chapter the Akedah, the Binding of Isaac, and it holds a place of great honor in Jewish prayer and reading, including at the New Year. Jews and Christians share reverence for this father of faith (Nostra Aetate 4).

The Lectionary leaves out the journey (vv. 3–8), which many people know best: the three days’ walk, Isaac carrying the wood, and his question, “where is the lamb?” Abraham’s answer there is, “God himself will provide the lamb for a burnt offering, my son” (22:8). A preacher may well read them, or tell them, on this Sunday. 2 Chronicles 3:1 identifies Mount Moriah with the place where Solomon’s Temple would stand.
str: vv. 1–2: the test and the command.
v. 9a: the place, the altar.
vv. 10–13: the knife, the angel’s voice, the ram.
vv. 15–18: the second call from heaven: God swears by himself and renews the promise.
¶ The reader is told at the start what Abraham does not know: “God tested Abraham”. So we are never in doubt about what God intends, and the story can hold our attention on Abraham’s obedience.
kw: A test in the Bible is meant to bring out and strengthen what is in a person, not to trip him. The same word is used of Israel in the desert (Exodus 16:4; Deuteronomy 8:2).

The answer of one who is fully available. Abraham says it to God at the start and to the angel in v. 11 (and to Isaac in v. 7, a verse not read today). Moses (Exodus 3:4) and Samuel (1 Samuel 3:4) give the same answer.

The only son of the promise, as Ishmael has by then been sent away (chapter 21). The Greek Old Testament translates this word in v. 2 as agapētos, “beloved”: the very word of the Father’s voice in today’s Gospel.
The verb of v. 9, “He bound his son Isaac”, from which the name Akedah comes. It is used nowhere else in the Hebrew Bible.
vv: Take your son, your only son Isaac, whom you love,
The words come slowly, each one tightening. God names the love, and so does not hide what he is asking.
But the angel of the Lord called to him from heaven, and said, “Abraham, Abraham!” And he said, “Here I am.”
The same words as v. 1. The name is called twice, as if in haste. God’s last word is not the command but the stopping of it.
for now I know that you fear God, since you have not withheld your son, your only son, from me.
“Now I know” is human language: God already knows, but in this act Abraham’s faith has become visible. “Not withheld” is the phrase St Paul will echo.
And Abraham looked up and saw a ram, caught in a thicket by its horns.
Something is given in the place of his son, and it was given by God. The verse that follows names the place “The Lord will provide” (22:14).
and by your offspring shall all the nations of the earth gain blessing for themselves, because you have obeyed my voice.

The promise reaches the whole world. A note on the text. The Hebrew verb can be read “shall bless themselves” or “shall be blessed”; the NRSV takes the first, and the POC the second (അനുഗ്രഹിക്കപ്പെടും). In Acts 3:25 Peter applies this to what God has done in Jesus.
ch: The Catechism says that Abraham’s faith, in this last purification, conforms “the father of believers” to the likeness of the Father who will not spare his own Son but will deliver him up for us all (CCC 2572). Hebrews 11:19 says of Abraham: “He considered the fact that God is able even to raise someone from the dead”. Origen and others among the Fathers saw in Isaac carrying the wood a figure of Christ carrying his cross (in substance). The likeness is real and so is the difference: for Isaac a ram is found, and for the Son of God there is no substitute, because he himself is the Lamb.

r.h: If God is for us
set: Paul wrote to the Christians of Rome, a community he had not founded, around AD 57–58, most likely from Corinth. Chapter 8 is the summit of the letter’s teaching on life in the Spirit. Verses 31–39 are its conclusion: a hymn of confidence in the form of questions, which ends with the certainty that nothing can separate us from the love of God in Christ.
str: v. 31b: the opening question.
v. 32: the proof: God has already given his Son.
v. 33: who will accuse? God justifies.
v. 34: who will condemn? Christ intercedes.

¶ The setting is a court of law, in which the accuser finds that the judge is on the side of the accused. In Greek vv. 33–34 can be punctuated in more than one way, as questions or as statements, and Bibles differ. The sense does not change.
kw: This is the verb of Genesis 22:12 and 22:16 in the Greek Old Testament. Paul is plainly thinking of Abraham.
The word is used for Judas’ betrayal and for the handing over of Jesus in the Passion accounts. Behind them all, Paul says, stands the Father’s gift.
To approach someone on another’s behalf. It is used of the Spirit a few verses earlier (8:27) and of Christ the high priest (Hebrews 7:25).
vv: If God is for us, who is against us?
Paul does not say that no one is against us. He has just spoken of suffering, and he will soon list hardship, famine and the sword (8:35). He says no one can finally stand against us.
He who did not withhold his own Son, but gave him up for all of us, will he not with him also give us everything else?

This is the argument at its strongest: God has already given the most he could give. There is no reason for him to refuse lesser things. Note “with him”: everything else comes with the Son, not instead of him.
It is Christ Jesus, who died, yes, who was raised, who is at the right hand of God, who indeed intercedes for us.
Four steps, rising: died, raised, at the right hand, interceding. This may echo an early statement of faith. The one person who could rightly condemn us is the one who is pleading for us.
ch: The Catechism quotes Romans 8:32 to teach that Jesus took on our condition out of love for us, and that the giving of the Son shows God’s plan for us to be one of benevolent love (CCC 603–604). It also teaches that Christ’s intercession is the foundation of all Christian intercession: he “always lives to make intercession” (Hebrews 7:25; CCC 2634, 2741). When we pray “through Christ our Lord” at Mass, we are joining a prayer already being offered.

r.h: This is my Son, the Beloved; listen to him!
set: The moment comes at the turning point of Mark’s Gospel. Peter has just confessed Jesus as the Messiah. Jesus has then said for the first time that “the Son of Man must undergo great suffering… and be killed, and after three days rise again” (8:31), Peter has protested, and Jesus has told all who would follow him to “take up their cross” (8:34).

“Six days later”: Mark rarely gives such an exact link, and this one ties the vision to those hard words. The mountain is not named. Christian tradition from early times has pointed to Tabor in Galilee; some scholars suggest Hermon, nearer to Caesarea Philippi. The Gospel does not tell us, because its interest is elsewhere.
str: vv. 2–3: the change in Jesus.
v. 4: Elijah and Moses.
vv. 5–6: Peter’s proposal and the disciples’ fear.
v. 7: the cloud and the voice.
v. 8: only Jesus.
vv. 9–10: coming down: the command to silence and the question.
kw: The word gives us “metamorphosis”. A passive: this is God’s doing. Paul uses the same verb for what happens in Christians (Romans 12:2; 2 Corinthians 3:18).
The word for the tents of the Exodus and of the Feast of Tabernacles. Peter may want to keep the moment, and to honor the three equally. He has not yet understood.
The same word is used of the cloud over the Tent of Meeting in the Greek of Exodus 40:35, and of the Spirit coming upon Mary (Luke 1:35). It speaks of God’s own presence.
It was said at the baptism (1:11) and comes again here, now for the disciples to hear. It recalls Isaac, the beloved son of Genesis 22:2 in the Greek.
This recalls Moses’ promise of “a prophet like me” (Deuteronomy 18:15; the Greek has the same words). And the last thing Jesus has said is about the Cross.
vv: And he was transfigured before them, and his clothes became dazzling white, such as no one on earth could bleach them.
Mark, with a homely touch, thinks of the laundry. This whiteness is not of earth. In Daniel 7:9 white clothing belongs to the Ancient One.
And there appeared to them Elijah with Moses, who were talking with Jesus.
Both met God on a mountain (Exodus 24; 1 Kings 19). They are often read as the Law and the Prophets. Elijah was expected before the great day (Malachi 4:5), and Moses had promised a prophet to come.
He did not know what to say, for they were terrified.
Mark is honest about the disciples. An early tradition connects this Gospel with Peter’s preaching, so this may be Peter’s own humble memory.
Then a cloud overshadowed them, and from the cloud there came a voice, “This is my Son, the Beloved; listen to him!”
The whole scene comes down to this one command. The Father does not say “build”. He says “listen”.
Suddenly when they looked around, they saw no one with them any more, but only Jesus.
The glory is gone and the great figures are gone. There is only the Jesus who will walk to Jerusalem. That is what the disciples have, and it is what we have.
So they kept the matter to themselves, questioning what this rising from the dead could mean.
The vision cannot be understood before the Resurrection, and neither can the Cross. That is why they are to tell no one “until after” (9:9).
ch: The Catechism teaches that for a moment Jesus discloses his divine glory, and so confirms Peter’s confession, and also that he will have to go by way of the Cross at Jerusalem in order to enter into his glory (CCC 555). It quotes St Thomas Aquinas: the whole Trinity appeared, the Father in the voice, the Son in the man, the Spirit in the shining cloud (CCC 555). St Leo the Great preached that the chief purpose of the Transfiguration was to take the scandal of the Cross from the hearts of the disciples (in substance; Sermon 51). 2 Peter 1:17 keeps the memory of the voice. The Transfiguration is also a promise for our own bodies, which will be conformed to his (CCC 556).

qa: Would God really ask someone to kill a child?

No, and the story itself says so: God stops the knife. The reader is told from the first line that this is a test, and its outcome is that God does not want the death of Isaac. Israel’s prophets later condemn child sacrifice in the strongest terms: “which I did not command, nor did it come into my mind” (Jeremiah 7:31), and the Church teaches that no one may ever claim the right to destroy an innocent human being (CCC 2258). No one today can take this chapter as permission to harm anyone, whatever voice they think they hear.
When Paul says God “did not withhold” his Son, does it mean an angry Father punished Jesus?

No. The Father and the Son are never set against each other in the Passion. Paul’s argument is that the gift of the Son proves how much God is for us. The Catechism says that God’s plan for us is one of benevolent love, which comes before any merit of ours (CCC 604). Jesus laid down his life of his own accord (John 10:18), and the love of the Father and the Son is one love.
Why did Jesus tell the disciples to say nothing?

Because “Son of God” and “glory” would be misunderstood without the Cross and the Resurrection. Until then the disciples themselves do not understand (9:10). The silence has a term: “until after the Son of Man had risen from the dead” (9:9). After Easter, it becomes the Church’s preaching.
rite: The Roman Church reads a Transfiguration Gospel on every Second Sunday of Lent, in all three years of the Lectionary, and the Preface of the day says why: Jesus, after telling his disciples of his coming Death, showed them his glory, so that the Law and the Prophets might witness that the Passion leads to the glory of the Resurrection (in substance). The first Eucharistic Prayer, the Roman Canon, names “the sacrifice of Abraham, our father in faith” just after the consecration, and so this Sunday’s first reading is not far from what happens on the altar. The Transfiguration is also a Luminous Mystery of the Rosary (St John Paul II, Rosarium Virginis Mariae, 2002), and it may be prayed this week for those who are preparing for Baptism at Easter.
study: Abraham obeyed without seeing where it would end. What is God asking of me now that I cannot see the end of?
“He who did not withhold his own Son”: where do I doubt God’s care for me? How does Romans 8:32 answer that doubt?
Peter wanted to stay on the mountain and build. What moments of consolation have I wanted to keep, and what is waiting for me back down the mountain?
“Listen to him.” What concrete time will I set aside this Lent to listen to Jesus in the Gospels?

lead: As Lent’s second week opens, the Church stops to keep a feast, and the violet gives way to white. The Chair of St Peter is not a feast of a piece of furniture. A chair is where a teacher sits and where a bishop presides, and this feast gives thanks for the service of teaching and unity that Christ entrusted to Peter.

The two readings show the two sides of that gift. In the Gospel, a fisherman is named a rock and given keys. In the First Reading, the letter under his name speaks to other elders as one of them, and it warns them not to “lord it over” anyone. Psalm 23 stands between the two: the true shepherd of the flock is the Lord. The key words are rock, keys and shepherd.

r.h: Tend the flock of God
set: This letter is addressed to Christians scattered across the Roman provinces of Asia Minor (1:1), people who were few in number and looked on with suspicion. Its great theme is how to stand firm in suffering. Now, near the end, it turns to those who lead these small communities.

The letter bears Peter’s name and the Church has always received it as Scripture under that name. Its closing mentions Silvanus, through whom it was written (5:12), and greetings from the church “in Babylon” (5:13), most likely a coded name for Rome. Many scholars think the polished Greek points to a helper or to a disciple writing in Peter’s name after his death. Others hold that the Silvanus of 5:12 explains the Greek. Either way, this is the voice of the Petrine tradition, and it comes to us from Rome.
str: v. 1: who is speaking: a fellow elder, a witness, a sharer in the glory.
v. 2: the task: tend the flock, with three contrasts (not forced but willingly, not for gain but eagerly).
v. 3: the third contrast: not as masters but as examples.
v. 4: the reward: the chief shepherd and the unfading crown.
kw: A word found only here in the New Testament. The leader of the apostles could have spoken from above. He chooses to stand beside the other elders.
The verb covers all that a shepherd does: feeding, guarding, leading. It is the verb the risen Lord uses to Peter at the lakeside: “Tend my sheep” (John 21:16). Peter now passes on what he received.
The same word Jesus uses of the rulers of the Gentiles in Matthew 20:25. It means to use authority for oneself, and Peter shuts that door on Church leaders.
Also found only here in the New Testament. Every pastor is an under-shepherd. The flock is “of God”, and it never becomes the property of the man who tends it.
vv: Now as an elder myself and a witness of the sufferings of Christ,

He could call himself apostle, as in 1:1. Here he appeals to what he saw: the sufferings. He was also the one who denied the Lord during those sufferings, and he holds the authority Christ gave him as one who has received mercy.
to tend the flock of God that is in your charge, exercising the oversight, not under compulsion but willingly, as God would have you do it

A note on the text. The words “exercising the oversight” (one Greek word, related to episkopos, bishop) are missing from some very old manuscripts. The NRSV keeps them, and the POC does not have them. The sense of the verse does not change.
Do not lord it over those in your charge, but be examples to the flock.

The Greek word behind “those in your charge” is klēroi, the portions allotted. The English “clergy” comes from the same root, yet here the word is used of the people. The pastor’s method is the example of his life.
And when the chief shepherd appears, you will win the crown of glory that never fades away.
The crown of the Greek games was a wreath of leaves that withered within days. This one does not fade. The pastor is not told to look for his reward in honor or income now.
ch: The Second Vatican Council took up this language when it taught that the bishops are to govern as vicars of Christ, in the spirit of service (Lumen Gentium 27). The Catechism says that the Good Shepherd ought to be the model of the bishop’s pastoral office (CCC 896). St Augustine put the balance in a famous sentence to his people, which the Council quotes: for you I am a bishop, with you I am a Christian (Sermon 340; Lumen Gentium 32). It fits this passage very well: an elder among elders, a sheep among the sheep, and still a shepherd.

r.h: You are Peter
set: Jesus has taken his disciples north, out of Galilee, to the district of Caesarea Philippi at the foot of Mount Hermon, near one of the sources of the Jordan. The town had been rebuilt by Philip the tetrarch and named in honor of Caesar, and the place was known for a cave and a shrine to the Greek god Pan. So in a region of other gods and of imperial power, Jesus asks who he is.

This is a turning point in the Gospel. Straight after these verses Jesus begins to speak openly of his suffering, and Peter, who has just been called a rock, tries to stop him and is told, “You are a stumbling block to me” (16:23). The reading stops before that, but it must not be forgotten: the rock is a man who still has much to learn. Mark 8:27–30 and Luke 9:18–21 also give Peter’s confession. The words about the rock and the keys are found only in Matthew.
str: vv. 13–14: what people say: John the Baptist, Elijah, Jeremiah, a prophet.
vv. 15–16: “But who do you say that I am?” and Peter’s answer.
v. 17: the source of that answer: the Father.
v. 18: the new name and the promise of the Church.
v. 19: the keys, and binding and loosing.
kw: A play on words. In Greek petra is a feminine noun, so a man’s name takes the form Petros. Behind both, Jesus’ own Aramaic very likely had one word, kēpā’, “rock”. That is why Paul and John call him Cephas (1 Corinthians 15:5; John 1:42).

In the Gospels the word appears only in Matthew (here and twice in 18:17). In the Greek Old Testament it often stands for the assembly of Israel (qāhāl). “My” church: it belongs to Jesus, and Peter is its steward.
Hades is the realm of the dead, not simply the place of the damned, though the POC translates “gates of hell”. Gates stand for the power of a city. Death itself will not prevail over this community.

The image comes from Isaiah 22:22, where the steward of the royal house receives authority: “I will place on his shoulder the key of the house of David; he shall open, and no one shall shut”. The holder of the keys acts for the king; he does not replace him.
Terms used in the Jewish teaching of that time for forbidding and permitting, and for imposing and lifting a ban. They speak of decisions with real authority.
vv: He said to them, “But who do you say that I am?”
The “you” is plural in Greek. Jesus asks all of them, and Simon answers for all. Opinions about Jesus are not enough, however respectful.
Simon Peter answered, “You are the Messiah, the Son of the living God.”
“Living” is a small word with weight in a place of carved gods. Mark has only “You are the Messiah” (Mark 8:29). Matthew’s fuller form reaches further.
Blessed are you, Simon son of Jonah! For flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father in heaven.
“Flesh and blood” is a Hebrew way of saying a mere human being. Peter’s insight is a gift. All faith begins this way (CCC 153 quotes this verse).
And I tell you, you are Peter, and on this rock I will build my church, and the gates of Hades will not prevail against it.

Abraham was once called the rock from which Israel was cut (Isaiah 51:1–2), and some interpreters hear that echo. A change of name in the Bible means a new mission, as with Abram and Jacob. The builder is Christ; “I will build” is his own promise, and so the promise depends on him rather than on Peter’s strength.
I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven, and whatever you bind on earth will be bound in heaven,

In 18:18 the power to bind and loose is given to the disciples together (“you” plural). The keys are said to Peter alone. The Catechism draws that distinction: Peter received a specific authority, and the college of apostles, united to its head, also received the power to bind and loose (CCC 553, 881).
ch: The Catechism teaches that the Lord made Simon alone the rock of his Church and gave him the keys, and that the Bishop of Rome, Peter’s successor, is the perpetual and visible source and foundation of the unity of the bishops and of the faithful (CCC 881–882, quoting Lumen Gentium 23). It explains binding and loosing as authority to absolve sins, to give doctrinal judgments and to make disciplinary decisions (CCC 553).

It also says that on the rock of the faith confessed by Peter, Christ built his Church (CCC 424). The Fathers read the rock in more than one way. St Leo the Great, whose sermon on Peter the Church reads in the Office of Readings on this feast, says that out of the whole world one man, Peter, is chosen (in substance). St Augustine, late in life, recalled that he had explained the rock sometimes as Peter and sometimes as Christ, and he left the reader to choose (Retractations, in substance). The two are not rivals: Christ is the foundation (1 Corinthians 3:11), and it is Christ who makes Peter a rock.

qa: Does “the rock” mean Peter himself or Peter’s faith?

The natural reading of the words is that Jesus is speaking of Peter, because the name and the promise come in one breath. Many non-Catholic scholars now agree with that. Catholic teaching does not separate the man from his confession: Peter is the rock as the one who confesses Christ (CCC 424, 552, 881). Other Christians understand this text and its application to the Bishop of Rome differently, and St John Paul II asked them to help seek a way of exercising this ministry that all could recognize as a service of love (Ut Unum Sint 95).
Was Peter ever in Rome? The New Testament does not say so plainly.

It does not narrate it, but the early witness is strong. 1 Peter 5:13 most likely points to Rome as “Babylon”. The letter of St Clement of Rome (about AD 96) speaks of the martyrdom of Peter and Paul, and St Irenaeus (about AD 180) names them as founders of the Church of Rome (Against Heresies 3). Excavations under St Peter’s Basilica found a small shrine of the second century, on the spot that Christians of that age honored as Peter’s memorial.
If the Pope is the rock, does that mean he cannot sin or make a mistake?

No. Peter himself is called a stumbling block five verses later and later denied the Lord. Popes confess their sins like other Christians. Infallibility is a much narrower thing: when the Pope, as supreme teacher, definitively proclaims a doctrine of faith or morals, the Holy Spirit keeps him from error, so that the Church stays in the truth (CCC 889–891). It does not extend to his private opinions or his practical decisions.
rite: Rome was already keeping this day in the fourth century. A Roman calendar of AD 354 lists it on 22 February. In the apse of St Peter’s Basilica, Bernini’s great bronze throne encloses an old wooden chair, and in early writers such as St Cyprian, “the chair of Peter” already stands for the Roman see. Because this is a feast, the Gloria is sung today although it is Lent, and white replaces violet, with the proper readings taking the place of those for the weekday. Latin, Syro-Malabar and Syro-Malankara Catholics in Kerala have three different liturgies and are one in communion with Peter’s successor. It is a fitting day to pray for the Pope by name, and for the unity of all Christians.
study: Jesus asks me, not only the crowds: “Who do you say that I am?” How would I answer in my own words today?
Peter is called a rock and, a few verses later, a stumbling block. What gives me courage in that? How should it shape the way I speak of the Pope and of my own pastors?
“Not for sordid gain but eagerly”: which of Peter’s three warnings speaks most to those of us who hold any authority, in a parish, a school or a family?
How often do I pray for the Pope and my bishop, and for the unity of the Church?

lead: Both readings deal with a religion that looks well and is hollow within. Isaiah, speaking to the leaders of Jerusalem, says: wash, learn to do good, and God will make scarlet into snow. Jesus warns against a piety done “to be seen” and points to another greatness: service. Neither reading is against worship or against teachers. Both ask that what we do on the outside should come from within. The key words are learn, justice and servant.

r.h: Though your sins are like scarlet
set: Isaiah preached in Jerusalem in the eighth century BC, when the small kingdom of Judah lay under the shadow of Assyria. Chapter 1 serves as an opening to the whole book, a kind of court case between God and his people. Just before our reading, the prophet says that but for a small remnant Jerusalem would have become like Sodom (1:9).

The Lectionary leaves out vv. 11–15, the hardest part. God says he has had enough of sacrifices and solemn festivals, “your hands are full of blood” (1:15). The point is not that worship is bad. Worship without justice is an offense to the God it honors.
str: v. 10: the summons, with a shocking form of address.
vv. 16–17: nine short commands: from “wash” to “plead for the widow”.
v. 18: God’s invitation and promise.
vv. 19–20: the choice: obey and eat, or refuse and be eaten.
kw: “Learn to do good.” Goodness is here a skill to be acquired by practice, like a trade. It does not come by a single fervent moment. Lent is a school of this.
Not an abstract ideal but right order in daily life, above all at the town gate where cases were judged. The orphan and the widow had no man to speak for them in that court, so God takes their side.

The verb comes from the law court: to settle a case by reasoning. The POC translates “let us be reconciled”, which gives the outcome of such a hearing. The judge himself invites the accused to talk it through, and he offers a verdict no one expected.
vv: Hear the word of the Lord, you rulers of Sodom! Listen to the teaching of our God, you people of Gomorrah!
The worst insult available: the rulers of the holy city are addressed as Sodom. The Hebrew for “teaching” here is tôrâ.
Wash yourselves; make yourselves clean;
Ritual washing was part of Israel’s worship. The prophet turns the word towards conduct: this is the washing that matters.
learn to do good; seek justice, rescue the oppressed, defend the orphan, plead for the widow.
The list comes down to names and faces. A test of a community’s religion is how its weakest members fare.
though your sins are like scarlet, they shall be like snow; though they are red like crimson, they shall become like wool.

Red dye of this sort held fast and would not wash out of cloth. What no effort of ours can remove, God can. Some scholars read the lines as a question, but the Church has always heard them as a promise.
ch: St Justin Martyr, writing around AD 150, quotes Isaiah 1:16–20 when he explains Christian baptism to the Roman authorities (First Apology 61). In Lent, a season that prepares for baptism at Easter and for the renewal of baptismal promises, the words fit well. The Catechism, speaking of the true worship of God, recalls that the prophets denounced sacrifices not offered from the heart or not joined to love of neighbor (CCC 2100). The Lenten call to almsgiving belongs here too: it is part of worship and not an extra.

r.h: The greatest among you will be your servant
set: Jesus is in the Temple in the last days before his Passion. This chapter is his last public speech in Matthew’s Gospel, and it is the sharpest. The scribes were the experts in the Law, and the Pharisees were a lay movement devoted to holiness in everyday life. Jesus shared much with them: belief in the resurrection, the practices of almsgiving, fasting and prayer, and calling God Father (CCC 575).

Many scholars think that the sharpness of Matthew’s wording also reflects the painful disputes between his own Christian community and the synagogue leaders of his day. This speech should never be used to paint the Jewish people, or Pharisees in general, in dark colors (Nostra Aetate 4; CCC 597). It is aimed first at Jesus’ own disciples, who are named in the first verse, and the warning passes to every Church leader since.
str: vv. 1–3: their teaching is to be obeyed; their example is not to be followed.
vv. 4–7: three faults: heavy burdens, display, love of honor.
vv. 8–10: three titles not to seek: rabbi, father, instructor.
vv. 11–12: the rule of the community: service and humility.
kw: Moses’ seat is the place of authority for teaching the Law. Stone seats of honor have been found in some ancient synagogues such as Chorazin, though these are later than Jesus’ time. Kathedra gives us “cathedral” and “ex cathedra”. Jesus does not deny the authority of the seat; he asks that the life of the one on it agree with it.

Small boxes holding verses of the Law, worn on the forehead and arm, following Deuteronomy 6:8 (in Hebrew, tefillin). The word is found only here in the New Testament. Jesus does not condemn them, only the wish to make them larger so that others notice.
One who serves at table and runs errands; our word “deacon” comes from it. In 20:26–28 Jesus will present himself as the model.
vv: therefore, do whatever they teach you and follow it; but do not do as they do,

A remarkable sentence, spoken by the one who is most severe with them. Authority does not depend on the holiness of the person who holds it. This protects the faithful when a teacher fails, and it gives no comfort to the teacher.
for they make their phylacteries broad and their fringes long.
The fringes are the tassels commanded in Numbers 15:38. Jesus himself wore them: the same word is used of the “fringe of his cloak” (Matthew 9:20). The fault is in lengthening them for show.
But you are not to be called rabbi, for you have one teacher, and you are all students.

A note on the text. The Greek says “you are all brothers”, and the POC has it (സഹോദരൻമാർ). The NRSV says “students” for the sake of the contrast with “teacher”, and notes the Greek in its margin. Both points are true: all are learners, and all are family.
The greatest among you will be your servant.
This is the heart of the passage. St Gregory the Great gave the bishops of Rome the title they still use: “servant of the servants of God”.
All who exalt themselves will be humbled, and all who humble themselves will be exalted.
The passive means God is the one who does it. Jesus says the same in Luke 14:11 and 18:14. Mary’s song says it too (Luke 1:52).
ch: The Second Vatican Council applies this directly to the Church’s own teachers: the teaching office is not above the word of God but serves it (Dei Verbum 10; CCC 86). In Lent the Gospel invites each of us, not only the clergy, to ask whose eyes we are living for. The same three practices are in view as in Matthew 6: done for the Father who sees in secret, or for those who are looking.

qa: Jesus says, “call no one your father on earth”. Why then do Catholics call priests “Father”?

Jesus cannot mean this as a ban on the word. He himself speaks of fathers and mothers in the commandment (Matthew 15:4). St Paul writes, “in Christ Jesus I became your father through the gospel” (1 Corinthians 4:15), and St Stephen addresses the Council as “brothers and fathers” (Acts 7:2). Jesus is using strong language, as he does when he speaks of plucking out an eye, against titles that are sought as honors or that put anyone in God’s place. A priest who is called “Father” should hear in it a duty of care. If he hears a claim to importance, this Gospel is for him.
study: Where has my faith become something done to be seen? What small act could I do this Lent that no one will ever notice?
Isaiah says “learn to do good”. Who are the orphan and the widow in my town, the people with no one to speak for them, and what is one thing I could learn to do for them?

lead: Today’s readings look towards the Cross by way of two men who are paying the price of their mission. Jeremiah’s enemies plot against him though he has prayed for them. Jesus, going up to Jerusalem, tells the Twelve what will happen, and on that very road two of them ask for the best seats. The answer turns our ideas of greatness upside down. The key words are plot, cup and ransom.

r.h: Is evil a recompense for good?
set: Jeremiah preached in Jerusalem from about 627 BC until after its fall in 587 BC. He warned that the nation was on its way to ruin, and for this he was regarded as a traitor. Earlier in this chapter he has gone to the potter’s house and heard God say, “Just like the clay in the potter’s hand, so are you in my hand” (18:6). The people answered that they would follow their own plans (18:12).

Our reading is part of a group of passages that scholars call Jeremiah’s “confessions”, or laments (for example 11:18–12:6; 15:10–21; 20:7–18). In them the prophet pours out his heart to God. Few other prophets let us see so far inside. The Lectionary stops at v. 20. In the verses that follow he prays for disaster on his enemies. It is an honest prayer from a man in pain, and it shows how far the Gospel will go beyond it.
str: v. 18: the plotters speak.
vv. 19–20: the prophet turns to God: listen; remember.
kw: The same word that God uses of his own plan in 18:11, and that the people use in 18:12. Human plans are set here against the plan of God, and they fail to overturn it.
The Hebrew of “let us bring charges against him”. The POC keeps this image (നാവുകൊണ്ടു തകർക്കാം). The first weapon raised against the prophet is talk.
A hole dug to trap an animal. Jeremiah will one day literally be let down into a muddy cistern (38:6).
vv: Then they said, “Come, let us make plots against Jeremiah

The speakers are not named. The next line shows that they are at ease with the religious order: priest, wise man and prophet, each with his proper gift. They are saying that the system will go on very well without him.
Give heed to me, O Lord, and listen to what my adversaries say!

They said, “let us not heed any of his words” (v. 18). He asks God to heed. When no one will listen to him, he brings it all to the one who will. The Catechism says that the prophets drew light and strength for their mission from such encounters with God (CCC 2584).
Is evil a recompense for good? Yet they have dug a pit for my life.
The hurt is personal, and the question has no answer.
Remember how I stood before you to speak good for them, to turn away your wrath from them.
This is what makes the pain so sharp. He had stood before God on their behalf, as Moses did (compare 15:1), and those he prayed for are the ones now digging.
ch: Christians have long seen in Jeremiah a figure of Christ: the innocent man, rejected by the leaders of his own city, who intercedes for them. People in Jesus’ day thought of him when they saw Jesus (Matthew 16:14). Jeremiah asks God to remember; Jesus goes further, saying, “Father, forgive them” (Luke 23:34). This also corrects a misuse of such texts: the plot is the work of particular men, and Jeremiah, like Jesus, belongs fully to the people he loves.

r.h: To give his life a ransom for many
set: This is the last stage of the journey. Jesus now speaks of his Passion for the third time in Matthew (after 16:21 and 17:22–23), and this third prediction is the most detailed. Only here among them does he say “crucified”.

Mark tells the same story with James and John making the request themselves (Mark 10:35–37). In Matthew their mother comes with them, kneeling. Her question comes straight after Jesus has spoken of mockery and flogging, and the Gospel lets us feel the gap between what he has said and what they have heard. She will appear once more, among the women looking on from a distance at the Cross (27:55–56).
str: vv. 17–19: the prediction.
vv. 20–23: the request and the cup.
v. 24: the anger of the other ten.
vv. 25–28: the teaching on greatness, sealed by the Son of Man’s own example.
kw: In the prophets the cup is often the cup of God’s judgment (Isaiah 51:17; Jeremiah 25:15). In the Psalms it can also be a cup of blessing. In Gethsemane Jesus will pray, “let this cup pass from me” (26:39).
The second word goes further than the first. A doulos belonged to someone else and had no rights. Jesus goes beyond “serve” to the very bottom of the social order.
The price paid to release a captive or slave. It is close in thought to the Servant of Isaiah 53, who “bore the sin of many” (Isaiah 53:12). In Hebrew usage “many” can be inclusive.
vv: then they will hand him over to the Gentiles to be mocked and flogged and crucified; and on the third day he will be raised.

Jewish leaders and Roman power both play a part in the story, and neither is the whole of it. The Church teaches that sinners, all of us, were the authors of the Passion (CCC 598). The prediction does not end in death. “He will be raised” is a passive: this is the Father’s work.
But Jesus answered, “You do not know what you are asking. Are you able to drink the cup that I am about to drink?”
He does not scold them. He asks whether they can share his way. They say, “We are able,” and they have no idea what they are saying, but he takes them at their word.
You will indeed drink my cup,

And they did: James was the first of the Twelve to be martyred (Acts 12:2). John, according to tradition, lived long and bore his witness in other sufferings. As for “right” and “left”, those two places are filled at Calvary: “two bandits were crucified with him, one on his right and one on his left” (27:38).
It will not be so among you;
A short sentence that has stood in judgment over Church life ever since. The Church has a different way of being great, or it has forgotten who founded it.
just as the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life a ransom for many.

The ground of the whole teaching. Jesus does not merely recommend service; he describes his own life. The Catechism says that “many” here is not restrictive: it contrasts the whole of humanity with the one Redeemer (CCC 605).
ch: This verse is one of the chief sources of the Church’s understanding of the Cross as a sacrifice for us. The Catechism sets it in the plan of the Father’s love and the Son’s willing gift (CCC 604–605, 608). It also grounds all office in the Church: ordination is a call to service, and those who receive it are servants of Christ and of the people (CCC 876). In the Latin text of the Mass the words over the chalice are pro vobis et pro multis, for you and for many, an echo of this same language.

qa: A ransom is paid to someone. To whom did Jesus pay it: to God, or to the devil?

The image should not be pressed that far. It tells us the cost of our freedom and who bore it; it does not name a receiver. St Gregory of Nazianzus raised this very question and refused both answers: the devil had no right to such a price, and the Father did not demand it as if he delighted in blood. He says the Father accepted it out of his plan of love, so that humanity might be made holy by the humanity of God (Oration 45, in substance). The Catechism also speaks of the Son’s willing love and the Father’s love as one (CCC 604, 606).
study: When have I, like the mother and her sons, come to Jesus with a request about myself just when he was speaking about something far greater?
Jeremiah had prayed for the people who now turned on him. Is there someone who has hurt me whom I can still “stand before God” for?

lead: Jeremiah sets out two ways to live, two kinds of trust, in the picture of a shrub in the desert and a tree by the stream. The Gospel then shows that picture in two lives, a rich man and a poor man, on either side of one gate. Psalm 1 has the same image of a tree by the water. What matters is where the heart rests and whom the heart sees. The key words are trust, heart and gate.

r.h: Like a tree planted by water
set: This passage is a short poem of the kind that Israel’s wise men wrote. It is very close to Psalm 1. It stands among the prophet’s words to Judah in the last troubled decades before 587 BC, when the kings looked for safety to alliances with the great powers, Egypt above all (compare Jeremiah 37:5–10).
In such a setting “mere flesh” is not an abstract phrase. It is a nation relying on an army. It also speaks to every one of us who rests his life on money, position or useful friends.
str: vv. 5–6: cursed: the one who trusts in mortals is like a desert shrub.
vv. 7–8: blessed: the one who trusts in the Lord is like a tree by water.
vv. 9–10: a further question: who can know the heart? God can.
kw: The key verb of the poem, used in v. 5 and v. 7. It suggests resting one’s whole weight on someone. Verse 7 uses it twice: “who trust in the Lord, whose trust is the Lord”.
Used of the heart in v. 9. It comes from the same root as the name Jacob, the one who tricked his brother. The heart is a Jacob, as it were, and even its owner is taken in.
Literally “the kidneys”. Hebrew speech placed a person’s deepest feelings there, and thought in the heart. The NRSV’s “mind and heart” is a fair modern way of saying that God sees all that is within.
vv: Cursed are those who trust in mere mortals and make mere flesh their strength, whose hearts turn away from the Lord.
The last line shows the real issue. Asking people for help is no sin; the sin is the heart’s turning away.
They shall be like a tree planted by water, sending out its roots by the stream.
What makes the difference cannot be seen: the roots. Both plants stand in the same heat.
in the year of drought it is not anxious, and it does not cease to bear fruit.
No promise is made that drought will not come. A Kerala reader who has seen the deep-rooted trees stay green in a dry March will understand this at once.
The heart is devious above all else; it is perverse

After the clear picture, the poem turns more troubling: we do not easily know which plant we are. In the Bible the heart is the center of the person and not only of the feelings. Jeremiah will hope for a day when God writes his law on the heart (31:33).
I the Lord test the mind and search the heart,
This is the answer to “who can understand it?” The thought can frighten, and it can also bring relief, since the one who knows all is the one who heals.
ch: The Catechism says that the heart is our hidden center, beyond the grasp of our reason and of others, and that only the Spirit of God can fathom and know it (CCC 2563). It also says that God must give us a new heart, since the human heart is heavy and hardened (CCC 1432). Lent is the season for that prayer. St Luke’s Gospel puts the same contrast on the lips of Jesus, in the blessings and woes of Luke 6:20–26.

r.h: At his gate lay a poor man named Lazarus
set: Only Luke has this parable. His Gospel speaks often about wealth and the poor, and the whole of chapter 16 is about money. It begins with the dishonest manager and goes on to “You cannot serve God and wealth” (16:13). Jesus is speaking to people who had scoffed at him. Luke describes them as “lovers of money” (16:14), but this was a fault found in every community, and it should not be turned into a portrait of a whole group.

Parables that end with a surprise in the next world were known in the ancient world, and many scholars think Jesus takes up a familiar kind of story. What is new is the second half, with its talk of Moses and of someone rising from the dead.
str: vv. 19–21: two men in this life.
v. 22: both die.
vv. 23–26: the reversal, and the chasm.
vv. 27–31: the request for the five brothers, and Abraham’s answer.
kw: The Greek form of Eleazar, “God has helped”. He is the only person given a name in any of Jesus’ parables, and this is not the Lazarus of Bethany. The rich man has no name in the story (“Dives” is only the Latin word for “rich”). God knows the name of the one no one noticed.

The NRSV says “to be with Abraham” and “by his side”; the POC keeps the Greek image (അബ്രാഹത്തിന്റെ മടിയിലേക്ക്). A place of honor at a banquet was reclining close to the host, in the fold of his garment, as in John 13:23. The man who longed for crumbs now has the best place at the feast.
The realm of the dead. In this story it is a place of torment, and the POC translates it “hell”. The Catechism discusses what this abode of the dead means (CCC 633).
vv: There was a rich man who was dressed in purple and fine linen and who feasted sumptuously every day.
Purple was a costly dye and fine linen a luxury. The text does not say he had done anything wicked. He has not cheated or struck anyone. That is the frightening thing.
And at his gate lay a poor man named Lazarus, covered with sores,

The Greek verb suggests he had been put down there. He is near enough to be seen every day. The sin is what the rich man does not do about what lies at his gate. Later he will call Lazarus by name (v. 24), so he knew all along who he was.
and send Lazarus to dip the tip of his finger in water and cool my tongue;
Even now he sees Lazarus as someone to be sent on errands.
Besides all this, between you and us a great chasm has been fixed,
In life, a gate could have been opened at any time. Now the gap is fixed. The chasm begins as a gate that stays shut.
If they do not listen to Moses and the prophets, neither will they be convinced even if someone rises from the dead.

Luke’s readers know someone has risen from the dead. Miracles do not force the heart. Those who do not hear the word about the poor in Moses (for example Deuteronomy 15:7–11) will not be moved by a vision either.
ch: The Catechism uses this parable to teach that the soul receives its reward or judgment immediately after death (CCC 1021), and, from the Lord's words on the judgment in Matthew 25, it warns that we will be separated from God if we fail to meet the serious needs of the poor (CCC 1033). It sees Lazarus in the hungry and the many today who lack the bare necessities (CCC 2463). St John Chrysostom preached a whole series of sermons on this parable, and the Catechism quotes him: not to enable the poor to share in our goods is to steal from them and deprive them of life; the goods we possess are not ours, but theirs (CCC 2446). The Second Vatican Council names the rich man as the one we must not imitate (Gaudium et Spes 27).

qa: Does this parable mean that rich people go to hell and poor people to heaven?

No. Abraham himself, in whose arms Lazarus rests, was “very rich” (Genesis 13:2). Wealth does not condemn; blindness does. The rich man is condemned for what he did not see and did not do. Nor does the parable promise heaven simply for being poor. It says that God is near those whom others overlook. Details such as the talk across the chasm belong to the story and are not a map of the next life, though the Church holds firmly to what the parable teaches: our choices in this life have a lasting outcome (CCC 1021–1022).
study: Where do my roots actually go? When a “year of drought” came for me, what did I find myself relying on?
Who lies at my gate? Whom do I see every day, on my way to work or to church, without really seeing?

lead: In both readings a father sends a beloved son, and those he is sent to plot his death in almost the same words: “Come now, let us kill him” (Genesis 37:20), “come, let us kill him” (Matthew 21:38). Joseph, stripped and sold by his brothers, is on his way to become the savior of his family. The son of the vineyard owner, thrown out and killed, becomes the rejected stone that holds up the whole building. The Lenten path leads to Good Friday, and the reader of Genesis knows it will not end there. The key words are beloved, heir and cornerstone.

r.h: Here comes this dreamer
set: The last section of Genesis (chapters 37–50) is one long story, the story of Joseph and his brothers. It tells how the family of Jacob, here called Israel, came to Egypt. Its great theme will be stated only at the end: human malice cannot defeat God’s plan.

The Lectionary leaves out Joseph’s two dreams (vv. 5–11), in which his brothers’ sheaves and then the sun, moon and stars bow down to him. These are what lie behind the mocking word “dreamer”. Jacob’s favoritism and Joseph’s telling of his dreams do not help matters. The family is real, and God works through it.
str: vv. 3–4: the father’s love and the brothers’ hatred.
vv. 12–13a: the father sends him.
vv. 17b–20: they see him from afar and plot.
vv. 21–24: Reuben’s rescue attempt; the robe and the pit.
vv. 25–28: Judah’s proposal; the sale; the road to Egypt.

¶ The account of who sold Joseph is not simple: Ishmaelites in vv. 25–27, Midianites in v. 28. Many scholars think two old tellings have been woven together. Judges 8:24 also treats the two names as overlapping.
kw: The exact meaning of passîm is uncertain. The Greek Old Testament understood it as many-colored, hence the famous “coat of many colors”. The only other person who wears such a robe in the Bible is the king’s daughter, Tamar (2 Samuel 13:18). It was a mark of rank, not of work.
Literally “master of dreams”, spoken with contempt. They want to see “what will become of his dreams” (v. 20). As the reader will discover, they themselves bring the dreams about.
A hollow in the rock for storing rainwater. The Psalms use the word for the place of death (Psalm 88:4), and the same word is used for Joseph’s prison in Egypt (Genesis 40:15; 41:14).
vv: Now Israel loved Joseph more than any other of his children,
The Bible does not hide the problem and does not approve of it. It shows how love given unequally can hurt a family.
They said to one another, “Here comes this dreamer. Come now, let us kill him and throw him into one of the pits;
Jesus’ parable uses nearly the same words, and that is surely why these two readings are paired.
and they took him and threw him into a pit. The pit was empty; there was no water in it.
A small detail with a meaning: in that dry land an empty pit means slow death by thirst. The next verse says, “Then they sat down to eat”.
What profit is it if we kill our brother and conceal his blood?

Judah’s motive is unattractive: profit. He will have a long journey to make. In chapter 44 he will offer himself as a slave in place of Benjamin. Readers who stay with the story can see conversion happen.
and sold him to the Ishmaelites for twenty pieces of silver.
Twenty shekels was the valuation of a male between five and twenty years old (Leviticus 27:5). Christian readers think of the silver in Matthew 26:15.
ch: St Stephen tells this story in his speech: “The patriarchs, jealous of Joseph, sold him into Egypt; but God was with him” (Acts 7:9). The Fathers often read Joseph as a figure of Christ: the beloved son sent by the father, stripped, sold, thought dead, and exalted to give bread to the nations. St Ambrose wrote a whole treatise on him. The Catechism draws from Joseph its teaching on providence and evil: “God intended it for good” (Genesis 50:20; CCC 312). God does not will the sin, yet he can bring a greater good out of it.

r.h: The stone that the builders rejected
set: Jesus is in the Temple during his last days. The chief priests and elders have just challenged his authority (21:23), and he answers with three parables, of which this is the second. Everyone hearing it would remember Isaiah’s song of the vineyard: “the vineyard of the Lord of hosts is the house of Israel” (Isaiah 5:7). Jesus’ opening words are drawn directly from it.

In Isaiah, the fault lies in the vines, which produce wild grapes. In Jesus’ parable the vineyard is good, and the fault lies in those entrusted with it. That is an important difference. Absentee landlords and tense relations with tenants were a familiar reality in Galilee in those days.
str: v. 33: the owner’s care.
vv. 34–36: the slaves sent and mistreated.
vv. 37–39: the son.
vv. 40–41: Jesus asks, and the hearers pass their own sentence.
vv. 42–43: the rejected stone and the transfer of the vineyard.
vv. 45–46: the reaction.
¶ The Lectionary omits v. 44, which some ancient manuscripts lack.
kw: Farmers working someone else’s land for a share of the harvest. They are stewards and not owners. The whole drama turns on their forgetting this.
“This is the heir.” The word links the Son to the promise. Hebrews says God appointed him “heir of all things” (Hebrews 1:2).
In v. 43 the singular means a people that produces fruit, not “the Gentiles” as a replacement people. The word here defines a people by its fruit.
vv: There was a landowner who planted a vineyard, put a fence around it, dug a wine press in it, and built a watchtower.
The owner has done everything that could be done. The list is drawn from Isaiah 5:2.
Finally he sent his son to them, saying, ‘They will respect my son.’
Sending him is a foolish thing to do by any human reckoning. No sensible owner would risk it. That is the point: God’s patience looks like folly.
So they seized him, threw him out of the vineyard, and killed him.

Mark has them kill him and then throw him out (Mark 12:8). Matthew and Luke reverse the order, and many see here the fact that Jesus died outside the city: “Jesus also suffered outside the city gate” (Hebrews 13:12).
The stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone; this was the Lord’s doing, and it is amazing in our eyes
From Psalm 118:22–23, a pilgrim psalm. The image shifts from farm to building, because the story of a dead son cannot end with death. The early Church loved this verse (Acts 4:11; 1 Peter 2:7).
When the chief priests and the Pharisees heard his parables, they realized that he was speaking about them.
Matthew tells us who the “you” of v. 43 is. The crowds, in the very next verse, hold Jesus to be a prophet.
ch: The Catechism draws on this parable to show that Jesus is the Son, distinct from the “servants” God had sent before him (CCC 443). The Second Vatican Council uses the vineyard image for the Church itself (Lumen Gentium 6). So the warning now falls on us. The question to the Church in every age is: where is the fruit? The vineyard belongs to someone else, and no office or inheritance can excuse a harvest withheld.

qa: Does this Gospel teach that God has rejected the Jewish people and given their place to Christians?

No. In its own context the words are addressed to the leaders who were challenging Jesus, as v. 45 says, and not to the people, who regarded him as a prophet (v. 46). The Catholic Church teaches that the Jews should not be presented as rejected or accursed by God (Nostra Aetate 4), and that the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable (Romans 11:29; CCC 839). Nor does the Church inherit the vineyard as an owner. The parable’s warning now stands over Christian leaders and Christian communities, who will be asked for the fruit (CCC 597–598).
study: Joseph’s story turned evil to good, slowly and over many years. In what painful part of my own life have I seen, or do I still wait to see, that “God intended it for good”?
What in my life have I been treating as my own, when I am really a tenant? What fruit might the owner be coming to look for?

lead: Micah ends his book with a wonder: “Who is a God like you?” The Gospel gives the answer in a story: this is a God like a father who runs. Both readings speak of sins thrown away and of a joy that no one could have earned. Psalm 103 says the same, today’s Lenten song of mercy. With the Sacrament of Reconciliation in view, these may be the two most encouraging readings of Lent. The key words are mercy, return and celebrate.

r.h: Who is a God like you?
set: Micah came from Moresheth, a village in the Judean foothills, and preached in the late eighth century BC, in the time of Isaiah. He is the prophet of the small farmer who is being squeezed by the powerful, and the prophet of “what does the Lord require of you” (6:8).

The final verses of the book form a kind of liturgy of prayer and praise. Many scholars think this closing section took its final shape later, when the people had come through disaster and were looking back in hope. The people first ask God to shepherd them. Then they sing.
str: vv. 14–15: a prayer: shepherd your flock; show us marvels as in the Exodus.
vv. 16–17 (not read): the nations are humbled.
v. 18: the great question.
v. 19: pictures of forgiveness.
v. 20: God’s promise to the fathers.
kw: who is a God like you?

The question plays on the prophet’s own name: Micah means “Who is like the Lord?” It recalls the song at the Red Sea (Exodus 15:11). There the wonder was God’s power. Here the wonder is his forgiving.
God’s covenant love, loyal and generous. It occurs in v. 18 (NRSV “clemency”) and again in v. 20 (“unswerving loyalty”). He “delights” in it: forgiving is what God enjoys.
A verb used of subduing enemies. Our sins are treated as enemies which God himself overcomes.
vv: Shepherd your people with your staff, the flock that belongs to you, which lives alone in a forest in the midst of a garden land;

A note on the text. The Hebrew word karmel means “garden land” and is also the name of Mount Carmel. The NRSV takes it the first way, and the POC the second (കാർമലിലെ). Either way the flock is small and alone, and looks with longing to the rich pasture of Bashan and Gilead.
As in the days when you came out of the land of Egypt, show us marvelous things.

A note on the text. The Hebrew reads “I will show him”, with God promising. The POC keeps this first person. The NRSV, noting that the Hebrew is difficult, adjusts the verse so that the people’s prayer continues. Both lead to the same point: God’s future will be like the Exodus.
He does not retain his anger forever, because he delights in showing clemency.
Anger is real in the Bible and it is passing. Mercy is what God delights in.
You will cast all our sins into the depths of the sea.

Just as Pharaoh’s chariots “went down into the depths like a stone” (Exodus 15:5). In the Bible the sea is the place no one comes back from. The sins will not be fetched up again. Jewish custom has honored this verse: at the New Year (Rosh Hashanah), many Jews go to a stream or river and pray these verses, in the rite called Tashlikh, “you will cast”.
ch: In the Roman Missal, an old prayer (the Collect of the Twenty-sixth Sunday in Ordinary Time) says that God shows his almighty power above all by pardoning and showing mercy. The Catechism agrees, saying that God displays his power at its height by forgiving sins (CCC 270). Micah’s question has its answer in the Sacrament of Reconciliation, in which a penitent’s sins are truly taken away.

r.h: This brother of yours was dead and has come to life
set: Chapter 15 starts with a complaint. Tax collectors and sinners are drawing near to Jesus, and the Pharisees and scribes grumble: “This fellow welcomes sinners and eats with them” (15:2). The concern of those who grumbled was to keep faith with God’s holiness, and they are not to be despised for it. Jesus answers with three parables of something lost and found: a sheep, a coin and a son. Only the third has a second son, and he stands for anyone who grumbles at mercy, then as now.

A father could divide property in his lifetime, but for a son to ask for it was like saying he wished his father dead, as many commentators point out. By the Law the firstborn received a double portion (Deuteronomy 21:17), so the younger son’s share would be about a third.
str: vv. 1–3: the occasion.
vv. 11–16: the younger son goes away and falls.
vv. 17–19: he comes to himself.
vv. 20–24: the father’s welcome.
vv. 25–30: the elder son’s anger.
vv. 31–32: the father goes out to him as well.
¶ The parable ends without telling us whether the elder son goes in.
kw: The word can mean wastefully, without saving anything. It gives no details. Only the elder brother speaks of prostitutes (v. 30), and he has not been there to see it.
Sin here is a kind of being outside oneself, and repentance is the beginning of being sane again. His motive is far from pure at first: he is hungry. The father does not ask about that.
A strong word: moved in the very bowels. Luke uses it of Jesus at the widow’s son (7:13) and of the Samaritan (10:33).
vv: So he went and hired himself out to one of the citizens of that country, who sent him to his fields to feed the pigs.

For a Jewish hearer, this was the bottom. Pigs were unclean (Leviticus 11:7). He has lost everything that made him a son of Israel. The “pods” of v. 16 are probably carob, poor food, which the POC translates as “bran”.
But while he was still far off, his father saw him and was filled with compassion; he ran and put his arms around him and kissed him.

The father saw him from far away, so he must have been watching the road. Commentators often point out that a dignified elderly man did not run in that culture. The kiss comes before the confession and before any change has been proved.
Then the son said to him, ‘Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you; I am no longer worthy to be called your son.’

He has come with a prepared speech (vv. 18–19), and he does not finish it. The part about being a hired hand is cut short. (A few ancient manuscripts add it here; the NRSV notes this.) The father is already speaking of other things.
put a ring on his finger and sandals on his feet.
The robe, the ring and the sandals all say one thing: this is a son. Slaves commonly went barefoot, and a ring carried a family’s authority (compare Genesis 41:42).
But when this son of yours came back,
“This son of yours”: he will not say “my brother”. And he said “working like a slave” of his own life at home (v. 29). He was in the house and still far off.
Son, you are always with me, and all that is mine is yours.
As gentle as anything in the Gospel. The father went out to the elder son exactly as he ran out to the younger. He has two lost sons, and he goes out to both.
But we had to celebrate and rejoice, because this brother of yours was dead and has come to life; he was lost and has been found.
“This brother of yours”: the father gives the word back to him. “Had to”: heaven’s logic of joy (compare 15:7).
ch: The Catechism says that this parable describes the process of conversion and repentance, “the center of which is the merciful father”, and goes through it step by step (CCC 1439). St John Paul II wrote at length on it in two documents, Dives in Misericordia 5–6 and Reconciliatio et Paenitentia 5–6. In the first, he stresses that the father’s love restores the son’s dignity. In the second, he gives time to the elder brother, in whom he sees our own selfishness and the divisions in the human family. This parable should never be read as a picture of Jews and Christians. The elder brother is any believer who stays at home and has forgotten that he is a son.

qa: If God forgives so generously, why do I need to confess to a priest?

The younger son did say the words out loud: “Father, I have sinned.” Forgiveness cannot be earned, but it has to be received, and we receive it as people with bodies and voices. Christ gave his Church the ministry of reconciliation (John 20:23; CCC 1441–1442, 1461). In the confessional, the priest acts in the person of the Father who runs and of Christ the Good Shepherd (CCC 1465). The sacrament is above all the embrace, the robe and the ring.
study: At this moment, am I more like the younger son or the elder? Do I feel myself still “far off” from God, or do I feel at home with him but angry about someone else?
What keeps me from going to Confession this Lent? How would the father in this story answer that?

lead: This Third Sunday of Lent, in the Year B readings, puts three great signs of God’s presence before us: the Law, the Cross and the Temple. The Ten Commandments are given by a God who has already set his people at liberty. The Cross, a scandal to all human reckoning, is the power and wisdom of God. The Temple, the pride of Jerusalem, points to a body that will be destroyed and rise in three days.

Psalm 19 is the response, with its answer, “Lord, you have the words of everlasting life”. The readings are also about how the worship and the life of a believer fit together, and that question touches every Christian who has come to Lent wanting something to change. The key words are word, foolishness and temple.

r.h: I am the Lord your God, who brought you out
set: Israel has come out of Egypt and reached Sinai. God has offered a covenant: “you shall be my treasured possession” (19:5). Thunder and lightning have shaken the mountain. Now God speaks directly. Everything else in the Law of Moses comes through Moses; these words are given to all (20:19; Deuteronomy 5:22).

The same commandments are repeated, with some differences, in Deuteronomy 5:6–21. Scholars discuss how the text grew. The Church’s concern is with what it says, and with the place that Jesus himself gives to it (Matthew 19:17–19). The shorter form of today’s reading leaves out vv. 4–6 on images and vv. 9–11 on the sabbath rest.
str: vv. 1–2: God names himself: the Liberator.
vv. 3–6: no other gods, and no idols.
v. 7: the Name.
vv. 8–11: the sabbath.
v. 12: parents, with a promise.
vv. 13–16: life, marriage, property, truth in court.
v. 17: coveting: the commands reach into the heart.

¶ The numbering of the ten varies. Catholic and Lutheran practice, following St Augustine, joins vv. 3–6 and divides v. 17; the Orthodox and Reformed count vv. 3 and 4–6 as two; Jewish tradition counts v. 2 as the first “word” (CCC 2066).
kw: The Hebrew name for them (Exodus 34:28, where the NRSV has “ten commandments”; Deuteronomy 4:13; 10:4), which became Decalogue in Greek. The Catechism points out the same thing: they are words spoken by God (CCC 2056).

The word is used only of God in this form. It is the jealousy of a spouse, a love that will not share. The POC’s word (അസഹിഷ്ണു) can sound harsher than the sense intended. The next verse shows the proportion: third and fourth generation, against the thousandth.

Sabbath is to be kept in memory. Deuteronomy 5:12 has “observe”, and it gives a different reason: “Remember that you were a slave in the land of Egypt” (Deuteronomy 5:15). Exodus points to creation, Deuteronomy to liberation. Together they make a rich theology of rest.

The verb is about taking human life unjustly. The NRSV’s “murder” is more exact than the older “kill”, which the POC keeps (കൊല്ലരുത്). Jesus goes further, to anger in the heart (Matthew 5:21–22), and the Church’s teaching on the dignity of life flows from this (CCC 2258–2262).
vv: Then God spoke all these words:

God speaks first. They are given as a word, and the people can answer. The Catechism notes that everything is said in the first person, “I”, and is addressed to a “you” (CCC 2063). The Hebrew “you” is singular: each one is addressed in person.
I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery;

The most important verse, and it is not a command. Before any law comes the gift. These are not conditions for being rescued; they are the way of life of those already rescued. The Catechism says that the Decalogue must first be understood in the context of the Exodus (CCC 2057, 2061).
but showing steadfast love to the thousandth generation of those who love me and keep my commandments.

The punishment spoken of in v. 5, to the third and fourth generation, is, as many commentators explain, about the span of one household living together. The steadfast love reaches past every horizon. Ezekiel 18:20 later makes clear that each person answers for his own sins.
Remember the sabbath day, and keep it holy.

This is the longest commandment, and its rest extends even to slaves, animals and foreigners (v. 10). It is an early and striking protection of those with no power. Christians keep this commandment’s meaning on Sunday, the day of the Resurrection (CCC 2175–2176; St John Paul II, Dies Domini).
Honor your father and your mother,
This opens the part about the neighbor. The words were spoken first to adults about aging parents, not only to children. It is also the first with a promise (Ephesians 6:2).
You shall not covet your neighbor’s house;
The last commandment no judge could ever enforce, for it deals with what no court can see. The law ends in the heart, where Jeremiah said God would write it (Jeremiah 31:33).
ch: St Augustine, quoted by the Catechism, says that as charity comprises the two commandments, so the Ten Commandments are given on two tablets: three concern love of God and seven the love of neighbor (CCC 2067). When Jesus is asked about life, he points to them first: “If you wish to enter into life, keep the commandments” (Matthew 19:17), and sums up all in the two great commandments (CCC 2055). They bind Christians still (CCC 2068, 2072), because they express what it is to be human before God.

r.h: Christ crucified, the power of God
set: Paul founded the church in Corinth, a busy Greek port city, and wrote to it about AD 54 or 55 from Ephesus (16:8). The community was splitting into parties around favorite leaders (1:12), and some were proud of their eloquence and knowledge. Paul’s answer is to put the Cross back in the center.

Crucifixion was the shameful death reserved for slaves and rebels. Cicero, a Roman orator, called it the most cruel and disgusting penalty. An old graffito scratched on a wall on the Palatine Hill in Rome, often dated around AD 200, shows a crucified figure with a donkey’s head, and mocks a Christian named Alexamenos for worshipping his god. So to proclaim a crucified man as Lord sounded absurd to everyone.
str: v. 22: what people look for: signs, wisdom.
v. 23: what Paul preaches: Christ crucified.
v. 24: how those who are called receive it: power and wisdom.
v. 25: the general rule.
kw: A trap, or something that trips someone up; our “scandal” comes from it. To many of Paul’s fellow Jews a crucified Messiah was a contradiction, since Deuteronomy says that one hung on a tree is under God’s curse (Deuteronomy 21:23; compare Galatians 3:13). Paul himself had once persecuted the Church (Galatians 1:13).
This word gives us “moron”. To educated Greeks, a god who suffered and died made no sense.
This is the whole difference. Faith does not rest on being cleverer or more religious; it rests on God’s call, to “both Jews and Greeks”.
vv: For Jews demand signs and Greeks desire wisdom,

Paul, a Jew himself, is not mocking anyone. He names the two good things that people reach for: proof of God’s action and understanding of the world. Both are good, and either can become a way of setting terms for God. Jesus was asked for a sign, as in today’s Gospel (John 2:18).
but we proclaim Christ crucified, a stumbling block to Jews and foolishness to Gentiles,
The verb form “crucified” in Greek is a perfect passive: the Risen One remains the Crucified One. Paul’s preaching does not soften the shameful part.
but to those who are the called, both Jews and Greeks, Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God.
Note the reply. To those who demand a sign of power, he gives power; to those seeking wisdom, wisdom. God gives them what they wanted, in a form they would never have looked for.
For God’s foolishness is wiser than human wisdom, and God’s weakness is stronger than human strength.
A startling way of speaking. God is neither foolish nor weak. Paul means: what looks like foolishness and weakness in God’s action is greater than our best.
ch: The Catechism turns to this text at a very difficult point. Faith in God the almighty can be put to the test by the experience of evil and suffering. It answers that God has revealed his almighty power in the most mysterious way, in the voluntary humiliation and Resurrection of his Son (CCC 272). St Ignatius of Antioch, on his way to martyrdom, wrote that the Cross is a stumbling block to those who do not believe, but to us salvation and eternal life (To the Ephesians 18, in substance). This is why a crucifix stands at the altar at Mass: we do not hide the very thing the world finds foolish.
